items.title: Sons of the sound: How Mfanstsipim incubated and nurtured Ghana’s contemporary gospel
items.description: A School, a sound and a new movement Contemporary gospel music emerged in Ghana in the early 1970s, marking a major development in the country’s Christian music. Churches had long used hymns, anthems, cantatas, indigenous songs and some western instruments, yet many conservative evangelicals still regarded rock, soul, disco and electric guitars as worldly. Through Noise of Joy, Joyful Way Singers and its link with Calvary Road Singers, Mfantsipim incubated and nurtured a challenge to these attitudes, proving the value of contemporary Christian music for evangelism, fellowship and spiritual formation. Noise of joy: The beginning of a new sound In July 1970, guitarist Emmanuel Lartey, now the Rt Rev Prof Emmanuel Y Lartey of Emory University, formed Noise of Joy with fellow students Joseph Quist, Kwame Kyeretwie Ofori, Henry Badoo, TVO Lamptey and James Walton, joined by girls from Wesley Girls’ High School. That September, a visit by Youth For Christ’s Teen Team affirmed what the group had begun. Rather than suppress the movement, the School embraced it: because ‘Methodism was born in song,’ tutors such as W Paul Grimble and E John Watson encouraged the group to perform at services and gatherings across Cape Coast, as did Clarice Garnett of Wesley Girls’, who also guided them. From noise of joy to Joyful Way Parallel groups followed, notably the Evangels, led by Adisadel keyboardist Emmanuel Kweku Frimpong (‘Odas’). On 15 January 1972, Noise of Joy and the Evangels merged, combining a Beatles-style guitar sound with piano-led music reminiscent of the Edwin Hawkins Singers, a mix Professor Joe-Nat Clegg-Lamptey called ‘like dynamite!’ As Rev Joseph Gyebi observes, Joyful Way’s use of popular forms challenged prevailing evangelical attitudes and reached young people. Taking the gospel beyond the school gates Joyful Way toured nationally in the 1972 Nationwide Love Mission and was heard on GBC radio. In 1974 it appeared on Break For Music and launched Explosion of Joy, its Boxing Day concert, which still draws about 4,000 patrons a year and may be Africa’s longest-running annual contemporary gospel concert. Joyful Way inspired Calvary Road Singers, founded around December 1976 with Rev Spencer Duncan as founding President. Duncan had become ‘born again’ at a Joyful Way programme at Adisadel in 1972. As Rev Ebenezer Markwei, a founding member, recalls, ‘right from the start, we wanted to be like Joyful Way.’ Later groups shared this aspiration, including New Creation, Come Back, Abundant Life, the Commissioned Family and, more recently, Team Eternity, whose founder calls Joyful Way ‘a template.’ Joyful Way and Calvary Road: Completing each other Calvary Road combined music with drama, prayer and preaching. Dr Kwame Owusu Dapaah-Afriyie introduced it to Mfantsipim around 1980, and it grew into a network of campus ministries. At Mfantsipim, a friendly, sometimes competitive rivalry fostered musical talent and leadership, producing a strong line of vocalists, keyboardists, guitarists and drummers. As Kojo Folson (Borax) – former Deputy Headboy, Calvary Road member and possibly Mfantsipim’s finest guitarist – puts it, ‘we did not necessarily compete with each other; we completed each other.’ Changing scenes and shifting tides From the mid-1980s, the groups’ fortunes in Cape Coast declined. Joyful Way decided to close its branches in 1985, and the Cape Coast branch’s attempt to survive was dealt a fatal blow in 1986, when it was banned from Wesley Girls’ after a disputed service. The Adisadel branch gradually faded, but the Mfantsipim branch carried on as Joyful Noise, forming affiliations with groups at Ghana National and Wesley Girls’, and resumed its original name when Joyful Way reversed its decision around 1996. Calvary Road, by contrast, was swept up in the charismatic church wave of the late 1980s and 1990s. More than a dozen churches emerged from it or were founded by its members, including Lighthouse Chapel, Living Streams, Harvest Chapel and New Creation Chapel, though its influence as an independent music ministry has since dwindled. From school groups to national artistes As noted, the groups produced notable musicians. From Joyful Way came TVO Lamptey, a leading gospel tenor; Patrick Osei-Hwere, arguably Ghana’s first recorded gospel rapper who also helped found Intellecto Choirofest, the inter-university mass choir festival; vocalists such as Luigi Maclean, Calvis Hammond, Seth Acquah, Elvis Bentil and Nana Yaw Ofori-Atta; and songwriters such as TVO Lamptey (Wonjie Oyi), Sackey Bennin (Osabarima), Justice Akushie (I’ve Found It) and the present writer (Wahenni). The Calvary Road tradition produced award-winners Nii Okai and the late Kofi Dua-Anto (KODA). Other old boys emerged outside the two traditions, notably Perez Music, a 2023 Vodafone Ghana Music Awards winner, trumpeter Frank Guildford and Rev Joseph Gyebi. Joyful Way’s honours include the 1988 ECRAG and 1990 PAFAM awards and recognition at the 2003 Ghana Music Awards for its ministry and the packaging of Barima Yesu, written by the present writer. Its tours have reached West Africa, the United Kingdom, Germany, the United States and Rwanda, and its 1979 visit to The Gambia led to the founding of Youth For Christ, Gambia. A living legacy at 150 Mfantsipim’s musical traditions, including Joyful Way and Calvary Road, have shaped alumni in ministry and secular careers alike, building discipline, teamwork, leadership and Christian service. On Saturdays, young men still rehearse in Mfantsipim’s Assembly Hall as Joyful Way, the Mfantsipim group, probably unaware of the history behind each session. Calvary Road’s legacy lives on through its churches and leaders. Ironically, churches that once resisted Joyful Way’s style now routinely use contemporary gospel music in worship. As Mfantsipim turns 150, its story honours the sons of the School who transformed not only the sound of Ghana’s gospel music, but also how faith is expressed and lived. [A fuller version of this article will be published in the Mfantsipim Speechday brochure] The author is Ace Anan Ankomah, Esq, FGA (MOBA’84), Lawyer and Music Hobbyist

items.title: US offers $20m reward for info on ‘Iran’s nuclear program’: CENTCOM
items.description: Washington is offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program, the US military said Friday, as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war. Read Also: Iran warns of wider war if US attacks after Trump election rout A State Department program, Rewards for Justice, “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community,” US Central Command said on X. The program was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests. In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges. It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward. Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear program. “If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida. “If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.” But the president also said Iran – which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war – is eager to end the conflict. “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said. Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting. And on Tuesday Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue. Earlier this week Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. items.title: La Marocaine Bouchra Hajij élue présidente de l'Union des confédérations sportives olympiques africaines
items.description: La Marocaine Bouchra Hajij, présidente de la Confédération africaine de volleyball (CAVB) et vice-présidente de la Fédération internationale de volleyball (FIVB), a été élue, vendredi à Dakar, présidente de l'Union des confédérations sportives olympiques africaines, en marge des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Cette élection est intervenue lors de l'Assemblée générale de l'Union, tenue en présence des présidents et représentants des confédérations sportives olympiques continentales. L'élection de Mme Hajij à la tête de cette instance continentale témoigne de la reconnaissance de son expérience dans la gestion des affaires sportives, ainsi que de ses efforts en faveur du développement du volleyball africain, du renforcement de son rayonnement international et de la consolidation de la coopération entre les institutions sportives du continent. Dans une allocution prononcée à l'issue de son élection, Mme Hajij a souligné que les priorités de son mandat porteront notamment sur la fédération des efforts des confédérations africaines, la défense des intérêts du sport africain auprès des instances internationales et le développement des infrastructures sportives. Elle a également mis l'accent sur la promotion du sport chez les jeunes et les femmes, dans l'objectif de renforcer la place de l'Afrique au sein du mouvement olympique international. Cette élection marque une nouvelle étape dans le parcours de Bouchra Hajij et contribue à renforcer la présence des femmes marocaines et africaines au sein des instances de décision du sport continental. items.title: Punjab Revenue Authority wants electronic invoice system at all hotels, restaurants
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) has sought all hotels and restaurants to be equipped with the electronic invoice monitoring system (EIMS) for timely payment of taxes. It was sought by the authorities in a meeting with the Hotels and Restaurant Association held here on Friday. During the meeting, matters concerning installation of EIMS in the hotel industry and tax compliance came under discussion. The meeting focused on measures to bring the entire hotel industry into the tax net and further broaden the tax base. The participants reviewed the EIMS installation process, technical requirements and challenges faced by hotels in implementing the system. The association office-bearers assured the PRA of its full cooperation in initiatives aimed at improving the tax system and promoting digitalisation. On this occasion, PRA Chairperson Moazzam Iqbal Sipra emphasised that issuing proper computerised receipts to customers against services provided was a legal requirement. He stated that with the cooperation of the business community, the tax system could be made simpler, more transparent and efficient. He further noted that expanding the tax net would encourage business activities and promote a culture of tax compliance. The chairperson also warned that business operators involved in fraudulent practices in the issuance of electronic receipts would be closely monitored and subjected to heavy penalties. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

items.title: Trump: Lesson for Nigeria, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: Donald Trump wanted the November 3 midterm elections to be about him. He said so repeatedly, urging Americans to vote as though his name were on the ballot. He wanted a Republican victory to demonstrate that his presidency still commanded popular support and that his influence over American politics remained firmly intact. Well, Americans took him seriously. Perhaps more seriously than he expected. Democrats have won control of both chambers of the United States Congress, delivering a major electoral setback to Trump and his Republican Party. Yet, as the results became clear, Trump reached for an explanation that seemed to contradict his own campaign message. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he declared: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The irony is difficult to miss. He had spent weeks asking Americans to treat the election as a verdict on his presidency. When the verdict went against him, he suddenly appeared to be distancing himself from it. He wanted the political benefits of making the election about him without accepting the consequences when voters delivered an unfavourable answer. For readers in Nigeria, it is worth explaining what America calls midterm elections and why they matter. In the United States, a president is elected for a four-year term, but congressional elections take place every two years. This means that halfway into a president’s tenure, Americans return to the polls to elect members of the legislature. These elections are called midterms because they take place in the middle of a presidential term. Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, while senators serve six-year terms, with approximately one-third of the 100 Senate seats contested every two years. Midterm elections do not determine who becomes president. The sitting president remains in office. Instead, voters decide which party controls Congress and, by extension, how much support or opposition the president will face in the legislature This gives Americans an opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with a president’s performance without waiting another four years. They can strengthen the president’s party in Congress or hand control to the opposition, making it considerably more difficult for the president to advance his legislative agenda. That is precisely what has happened to Trump. American presidents often benefit from what is known as the coattail effect. When a president is popular, candidates from the same party can benefit from that popularity. His political strength becomes an advantage for others seeking elective office. But when a president becomes unpopular, the effect can work in reverse. Candidates associated with his administration may find themselves paying the price for public dissatisfaction with his leadership. In political terms, this is sometimes described as negative or reverse coattails. Trump’s decision to place himself at the centre of the midterm campaign made this effect particularly consequential. Instead of allowing individual Republican candidates to make their own cases to voters, he encouraged Americans to judge them through the prism of his presidency. He effectively turned hundreds of congressional contests into a national assessment of his administration. And voters had reasons to be dissatisfied. The cost of living, inflation, rising fuel prices, economic anxiety and concerns about his administration’s policies, including the war with Iran, featured prominently in the political atmosphere surrounding the election. The Associated Press’s voter analysis identified frustration over high costs and the direction of the administration among the forces behind the Republican setback. Not every voter necessarily shared the same grievance, but the cumulative dissatisfaction proved politically damaging. The scale of the Democratic victories was particularly striking in traditionally Republican territory. Texas provided one of the clearest illustrations. For decades, the state had been one of the Republican Party’s most dependable strongholds. Yet Democrat James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton in the Senate contest, becoming the first Democrat elected to a Texas Senate seat since 1988. In the gubernatorial race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott, ending Republican control of the governorship. These were not merely victories for individual candidates. They challenged the assumption that established Republican strongholds were beyond the reach of Democratic competition. One election does not permanently change a state’s political identity, but it can expose the vulnerability of a party that has grown accustomed to treating certain constituencies as guaranteed territory. The election also produced historic breakthroughs in American political representation. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of an American state. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the United States Senate. Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is positioned to become the first Black Speaker of the House if formally elected by the incoming Democratic majority. These achievements extend beyond party victories; they represent significant milestones in the country’s political history. But beyond the personalities and historic milestones, the institutional consequences are substantial. With Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump will face a Congress less willing to accommodate his agenda. The new majority can obstruct legislation, scrutinise government spending, investigate the administration and subject presidential appointments requiring congressional approval to greater scrutiny. Control of the Senate is particularly important because of its role in confirming federal judges and senior government officials. Trump remains president and retains his constitutional powers, including the power to veto legislation. A Democratic Congress cannot simply remove him from office or take over the executive branch. But the political environment in which he must govern has changed considerably. The final two years of his presidency will be more complicated, and his administration will have to contend with an opposition that now controls the legislative machinery. The results also raise questions about the future of the Republican Party. Trump’s endorsement has long been a powerful instrument in Republican politics. Candidates have sought his support, elected officials have adjusted their positions to accommodate his preferences, and the party has increasingly organised itself around his political identity. But when candidates associated with a president begin losing elections on a significant scale, an uncomfortable question emerges: is his influence still an electoral advantage, or has it become a liability? The answer will matter as Republicans consider their political direction beyond Trump’s second term and the road to the 2028 presidential election. None of this means that Democrats have secured a permanent realignment of American politics. Nor does it automatically determine who will win the next presidential election. Midterm results are not a crystal ball. They reflect the political mood at a particular moment, and voters can change their minds again. The Democratic Party must also demonstrate that winning control of Congress can translate into meaningful improvements in people’s lives. Defeating an unpopular administration and earning lasting public confidence are two different challenges. There is, however, a lesson here for political leaders everywhere, including in Nigeria. Elections are not always about the candidates whose names appear on the ballot. Sometimes, voters use the choices available to them to pass judgment on the person already occupying the highest office. A president may not be contesting, but his record, policies and conduct can still become the central issue in an election. Political power does not insulate an incumbent from electoral accountability, even when his name is nowhere on the ballot. Trump invited Americans to make the midterm elections a referendum on his presidency. They did. When the result went against him, he insisted that his absence from the ballot was the problem. But he cannot have it both ways. He wanted the credit if Republicans won. He cannot so easily disown the verdict because they lost. The slingshot has turned in the opposite direction. Trump asked Americans to vote as though he were on the ballot. They did something more consequential: they voted on the presidency he was already exercising. He asked for a political endorsement and received an electoral verdict. The post Trump: Lesson for Nigeria, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: From open pavilion to nation of orderlies: Is Zik’s ‘fear-free’ Nigeria still possible?
items.description: .What a 1960 inauguration says about fear in today’s corridors of power By Omeiza Ajayi Nearly 66 years after Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe was sworn in as Nigeria’s first African Governor-General, the footage of that day – which has again recently gone viral – raises an uncomfortable question: why did a leader who held the highest office in the land need no retinue of security details standing behind him, while today every minister, and even some local government supervisors, cannot move without a swarm of details? The inauguration took place on November 16, 1960, at Tafawa Balewa Square, barely six weeks after independence. It was also Zik’s 56th birthday. The narrator of the newsreel set the scene plainly. “At the steps of the pavilion stand the Prime Minister and the Lord Chief Justice, symbolising the people and the law, on what is surely one of the most important occasions in the history of the country.” No armed escort looms in the frame. No aide hovers at the shoulder of the man the crowd was chanting for. “Zik! Zik!” rang around the square as he arrived, and the vast stands, in the narrator’s words, were “hushed.” Today the picture is reversed. In Abuja and in the state capitals, orderlies trail ministers into halls and offices. The situation is so bad that some security personnel actually enter into very enclosed spaces or rooms with their AK47 rifles in clear breach of security protocol. At the local government level, some unelected supervisory councillors have been known to move with armed vigilance team members or hunters, sometimes to intimidate the very people they were appointed to serve. The easy explanation is insecurity, and it is not a false flag. Banditry, kidnapping and insurgency have made parts of the country dangerous, and no leader can be faulted for fearing for his life. But the leaders of other nations also face threats. Behind the American president or a British prime minister stand trained protective officers, assigned to a defined danger. They do not crowd every public official, from the cabinet room to the ward office, with men whose chief duty is to announce importance. It is not uncommon in Nigeria to see security details standing and blocking a television camera. That leaves the harder question. Are Nigeria’s leaders afraid of the general state of the country, or have they become afraid of their own people? Zik, standing in the open that November morning, appeared to have settled that question for himself. He began his address with these words: “It is with humility, mingled with joy, that I thank this grand concourse of patriots and friends of Nigeria for congregating here today on the occasion of my inauguration as the first African Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Federation of Nigeria.” He titled the speech “Respect for Human Dignity,” and he made no secret of what he feared for Nigeria. It was not assassins. It was division. “I appeal to all our leaders, far and near, to forget the wounds which were inflicted in cause of our internecine altercations. The love of our country should outweigh the love of our petty selves”, he said. He named his rivals one by one, among them Alhaji Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, and Chief Obafemi Awolowo, and invited them into what he called “this herculean task of national reconstruction.” A man who expects to be harmed by his rivals does not call them to his side before a crowd of thousands. His vision was explicit. “Let us bind the nation’s wound, and let us heal the breaches of the past, so that in forging our nation, there shall emerge on this continent a hate-free, fear-free, and grief-free people.” Fear-free was the promise. Sixty-six years on, the country has more roads, more universities and more money than that crowd could have imagined, yet fear now sits in the offices meant to dispel it. It sits with the minister who cannot cross a lobby unescorted, and with the local government chief who needs hunters to face his own community. It also sits with the citizen who cannot get near either of them. Nigeria’s innocence has long been defiled by rapists who sodomized her without protection. Today, we have a multitude of prostitue followership. The problem cuts both ways – a deceptive leadership and an ignorant followership. Much of what Zik said that day still holds. “Nigerians believe passionately in the fundamental human rights,” he declared, and he warned that “we must jealously guard our freedom with our lives, if need be.” The words read today less like history than like an assignment left unfinished What has changed is the distance between the governed and those who govern. In 1960, the footage shows a leader and a people with nothing between them. In 2026, the orderly has become the thing between them, a badge of rank as much as a shield. Whether Nigeria can return to the open pavilion depends on whether its leaders can once again be trusted by the people, and can trust them in return. Security is a necessity, but it cannot replace that trust. Zik believed the country could be “hate-free, fear-free, and grief-free.” The film of that November morning still plays, and it still asks of every leader who passes a crowd with armed men at his back: “The love of our country should outweigh the love of our petty selves.” Vanguard News The post From open pavilion to nation of orderlies: Is Zik’s ‘fear-free’ Nigeria still possible? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Daddy Showkey: Vanguard Award will be the biggest of my lifetime
items.description: By Clifford Ndujihe & Benjamin Njoku Chief John Odafe Asiemo, 57, popularly known as Daddy Showkey, is a household name in Nigerian music scene. He is the creator of ‘Galala’ music, which sound helped define Nigeria’s street music in the 90s. Read Also: Nostalgia, glitz as icons reunite for Daddy Showkey’s 50th anniversary celebration Daddy Showkey is a nominee for Vanguard Newspaper’s 2026 Entertainment Icon of the year award. Speaking with ululation after being presented with the letter of nomination, on Tuesday at his Lagos residence, he said: “They say a prophet is not recognised by his own people. But I am a prophet who is being recognised by the people who built me. This is the greatest awards I have ever received in my life because it is coming from Vanguard. Vanguard is the first newspaper in Nigeria that wrote about me, when I was nothing. This is Vanguard, and I cherish it a lot. “Apart from that, Vanguard played a big role in pushing me to the limelight. “So, a recognition award coming from Vanguard, I must cherish it. It is like my own people saying it is high time. Sometimes, when I see Vanguard giving people awards, I always say in my mind, when is it going to be my turn? “Now, it is my turn to receive the award and I am very grateful.” Reminiscing on his early days, Daddy Showkey, who celebrated 50 years on the stage recently, continued: “For years, I kept coming to Vanguard head office, but I never met the publisher, Uncle Sam, in person. After my secondary education, I hit the streets. From childhood, I had made up my mind to follow music. At 13, in 1983, I started following Danladi Bako of NTA. I was always at his office on Lagos Island. He would give me a voucher to go and eat, and made me comfortable in his office. My first song, “Big Belle”, was released in 1990 in Nawfia, Njikoka, Enugu-Ukwu, Anambra State. I cannot forget the late Amadi Ogbonna(former Vanguard Entertainment Editor). He was one of the earliest journalists to write about me and played a huge role in my career. Before Ogbonnaya wrote about me, we used to walk from Kirikiri to Olodi areas, passing Vanguard. I remember saying one day while walking past Vanguard ‘this newspaper will one day write about me.’ It came to pass when Ogbonnaya wrote about me for the first time. The second was Smart Irewudo, a former Champion Newspaper reporter, now based in the United States. Before I started recording, during the June 12 crisis, I led Ajegunle boys who blocked roads and extorted money from motorists. Smart took my picture and published it in the Daily Champion. In his mind, he thought he had done me a great favour. He didn’t know the police would come after me. Luckily, one of the policemen from Area F showed my picture to Amadi Ogbonna. He recognised me immediately and called me. When I showed up, Ogbonna took me to the police station and told them I wasn’t a bad boy, they should release me and focus on arresting real criminals. That same week in 1999, Dr Obiefula Nwankwo offered to record my songs. On the day I signed as his artiste, Amadi Ogbonna and Smart Irewudo accompanied me. After signing the deal, we ended up at the Vanguard Canal. That’s where we celebrated it. Ogbonna kept encouraging me, supporting my career financially and otherwise. If Vanguard decides to honour me today, I would say I merit it. It is Vanguard honouring their own, recognising their own pikin. And it will be the biggest award I will ever receive in my lifetime.” Vanguard News The post Daddy Showkey: Vanguard Award will be the biggest of my lifetime appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Police rescue 10 stolen children in Abia
items.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—The Abia State Police Command has arrested suspects linked to the October 17 attack on Uratta Divisional Police Headquarters, rescued 10 stolen children and recovered 15 firearms and 30 stolen vehicles in a major security crackdown across the state. The Command also disclosed that it arrested 109 suspects, comprising 89 males and 20 females, in connection with 211 criminal cases recorded between September 11, 2026 and November 6, 2026. Commissioner of Police, CP Wilfred Afolabi, who disclosed this on Friday while presenting the Command’s operational scorecard, said the arrests followed intelligence-driven operations and collaboration with other security agencies. On the Uratta police station attack, Afolabi said investigations had led to the arrest of some of the suspected attackers, with one of them allegedly confessing to leading the gang that carried out the assault. He said investigations were ongoing to track down other accomplices and establish the full circumstances surrounding the attack. In a related security operation, operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Unit raided a location at Ubakala, Umuahia South Local Government Area, on October 25, arresting a suspect identified as Osita. The police reportedly recovered two locally fabricated guns, 16 live cartridges and four expended cartridges from the suspect. Another suspect, 30-year-old suspect, was subsequently arrested for allegedly supplying ammunition illegally. Both suspects have been charged to court, according to the CP. On child trafficking, Afolabi said police operatives rescued 10 children during the period under review and reunited them with their families. He specifically disclosed that two suspects, including a 38-year-old , were arrested on October 11 over the alleged stealing of two children, seven-year-old Chiamaka Chikeze and nine-month-old Goodluck Chikeze. The children were reportedly recovered and handed back to their parents, while the suspects were charged to court. The police boss also announced the arrest of a five-man vehicle theft syndicate, aged 43, and 40. A Toyota Corolla with registration number ROU 9338J was recovered from the suspects, who have also been charged to court. In another operation, two suspected cultists, aged 27, and 25, were arrested on October 31 for allegedly dispossessing students of Abia State University, Uturu, of their mobile phones and other valuables at gunpoint. A locally fabricated firearm was recovered from them. The CP said one of the suspects had confessed to belonging to the Black Axe Confraternity, adding that efforts were ongoing to apprehend other members of the gang. Vanguard News The post Police rescue 10 stolen children in Abia appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Exchange rate’s woeful tale
items.description: THE preoccupation of exchange rate fundamentalists in Pakistan with a single, partial indicator — Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) — is astonishing. As Nadeem ul Haque argued in an illuminating article, fixing or deliberately boosting exchange rates effectively ended with Bretton Woods’ collapse in the 1970s. Research has since confirmed that the exchange rate is a market price — the price of one currency in terms of another, determined by underlying economic conditions — and not a policy tool. Hence, the exchange rate is an endogenous variable reflecting domestic inflation, productivity, external balances, capital flows, reserve adequacy, fiscal credibility, interest-rate differentials, and market expectations. As Haque notes, “The rupee does not weaken because someone decides to weaken it. It weakens because underlying conditions make the existing price unsustainable.” REER has a legitimate but limited purpose. It measures changes in the nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price movements against trading partners. But an index reading of 100, based on a selected base year, doesn’t establish an optimal exchange rate. Nor does a deviation from 100 automatically signal overvaluation or undervaluation. REER says little about balance-of-payments sustainability, foreign exchange availability from non-trade sources or exporters’ ability to compete through quality, technology, productivity, and delivery. There are questions to address before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy. First, does the base year 2010 represent an equilibrium exchange rate? Pakistan recorded a current account deficit of $3.95 billion, around two per cent of GDP, that year, compared with a near-balanced account in 2026. Second, have trade weights and trading partner composition remained representative over 16 years, especially after the China FTA? Third, have movements in individual partners’ currencies been adequately reflected in an index referencing the US dollar? Fourth, the choice of price deflator (CPI, PPI, unit labour costs or GDP deflator) can produce very different results. These points need serious thought before prescriptions are based on a single index. REER doesn’t capture many of the external account components. Workers’ remittances have grown faster than merchandise exports. They’re a major source of foreign exchange, financing imports of raw material, equipment and fuel, enabling domestic industry to use productive capacity that would otherwise be underemployed. They help build reserves, boost external stability, and reduce reliance on borrowing. FDI, portfolio investment, and external debt disbursements provide more foreign exchange liquidity. Assessments limited to REER overlook these determinants of external sustainability. Questions must be addressed before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy. Three empirical tests help establish whether the exchange rate is artificially managed or broadly market-determined. The first is the differential between official interbank and open-market rates. It peaked at Rs10-15 per dollar in FY2023. As reserves accumulated and market conditions normalised, the gap narrowed to its customary Rs0.50-2 range, indicating a more unified foreign exchange market. The second test is whether administrative restrictions on imports and profit and dividend repatriation are being used to suppress foreign exchange demand. Such curbs were imposed in FY2023 when SBP reserves fell to $3bn or so. Imports declined to $53bn and profit and dividend repatriation to just $331 million against normal levels of about $70bn and $2bn. Last fiscal, imports recovered to $71bn. Profit and dividend remittances reached $2.3bn. Arrears were cleared and current obligations met. This restoration hardly supports the view that the exchange rate is being sustained through administrative demand suppression. The third, perhaps most compelling, test is whether SBP has depleted its reserves to defend a parity. In FY2023, reserves fell to about $3bn recovering to around $21bn despite annual external debt-servicing dues of about $25bn. This accumulation occurred while the rate was around Rs280 per dollar and REER above 100. It’s difficult to reconcile this outcome with the claim that an artificial exchange rate is being maintained when SBP is mopping up surplus dollar liquidity after interbank clearance. Historical comparisons reinforce this view. Bet­ween 2015 and 2018, the rupee was maintained aro­­und Rs104 per dollar, but SBP reserves dec­li­ned from $18bn to $9bn. In contrast, in 2000-2007 when reserves increased from barely $1bn to $13bn, the exchange rate remained stable around Rs60 and exports more than doubled from $9bn to $19bn. Still, critics said the rate was artificially defended, overlooking the net foreign exchange inflows being sterilised to prevent excessive appreciation and protect exporters’ competitiveness. Market expectations are another important aspect. In Pakistan, they are often driven by a bandwagon effect instead of rational assessments of fundamentals. When reserves fall below comfortable levels, depreciation expectations can become self-fulfilling. Exporters withhold dollar proceeds within the permitted 90-day surrender period, anticipating a better rate; importers advance foreign exchange requirements to avoid future depreciation. Supply contracts and demand rises putting pressure on the rupee. The anticipated depreciation then materialises. Would a 10pc depreciation advocated by REER fundamentalists improve competitiveness? Foreign buyers may demand price discounts of at least 5pc from exporters, treating additional rupee earnings as a windfall. About 40pc of exports use imported inputs including fuel, LNG, and textile raw materials. Their costs rise, leaving exporters with a net gain of perhaps only 2-3pc. The impact goes beyond exporters. Costlier imports fuel inflation, hurting poorer households whose main asset is their labour and whose wages, particularly in an informal economy with extensive underemployment, do not adjust proportionately. The central bank may raise interest rates, increasing domestic borrowing costs. Imported machinery becomes costlier, forcing investors to put off or abandon projects, hurting both investment and growth. As the rupee cost of servicing external debt increases, partly offset by higher import-duty collections, government may have to borrow more, crowding out private-sector credit. Foreign investors earn lower dollar returns, discouraging fresh investment. The lesson is that exchange-rate stability can’t be engineered through administrative intervention or depreciation alone. It must rest on credible fiscal management, a broader tax base, sound trade and tariff policies, remunerative energy pricing, higher productivity and prudent monetary management. Together, these policies reduce the need for disruptive exchange-rate adjustments. Pakistan must not treat REER as a magic number and depreciation as a remedy. The aim should not be an arbitrary index reading but sustainable external competitiveness, stronger reserves, higher exports and investment, and protection of purchasing power. The exchange rate is a reflection of economic fundamentals, not a substitute for them. Correcting symptoms while neglecting underlying weaknesses will only perpetuate the rupee’s woeful tale. The writer is a former State Bank governor. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

items.title: ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The All Progressives Congress APC has told the Senator David Mark-led faction of the African Democratic Congress ADC to go sort out its internal mess and quit its “senseless rants” after a Federal High Court judgment sacked the faction’s leadership. Read Also: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate? In a statement Friday in Abuja, the APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the ruling party had no hand in the case. “To be clear, APC is neither a party nor an interlocutor in the matter. Nothing about the case has anything to do with the APC. And the APC has absolutely no role in the party’s judicial quagmire,” he said. The judgment, delivered on Thursday by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, sacked the David Mark-led leadership of the ADC. It also nullified all official acts of that leadership, including its primary election processes and outcomes, like the presidential candidacy of former vice president Atiku Abubakar. Morka said the case was brought by ADC national officers against the faction now removed from office, describing the suit as “a notorious case initiated by leaders of ADC against pirate leaders of ADC.” He accused Mark and his associates of taking over the party “to satisfy Atiku Abubakar’s quixotic presidential ambition.” According to him, “it didn’t matter to them that their hostile takeover of that party was in flagrant violation of the rule of law and ADC’s internal democracy, as a court of competent jurisdiction has now declared.” The APC spokesman also accused the ADC of reacting to court decisions according to whether they favour it. “Every time a court decides against the Senator David Mark-led factional African Democratic Congress, they accuse the All Progressives Congress of collusion and deprecate the judiciary. Every time a court decides in their favour, they hail the rule of law and extol the judiciary,” he said. He added that the faction’s attitude showed “no iota of regard for the authority and independence of the judiciary, an indispensable pillar of any democracy.” On Thursday’s ruling, Morka said it “was procured by their own lawlessness and demonstrates the vibrancy of the rule of law and independence of the judiciary in Nigeria.” He said the ADC leaders “take no responsibility or accountability for the self-inflicted injury that the court only judicially certified.” Vanguard News The post ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: I’ll ask my father, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: (Part 2) Authority, Loyalty, and the Unsettled Place of the Stepfather Last week, I examined the emotional burden placed on stepmothers in reconstituted families. But the other side of the same household tells a different story. What happens when a stepfather is expected to provide for a family but finds his authority repeatedly questioned? The scene plays out in thousands of living rooms every evening. A stepfather sits at the head of the table, looks at a teenager who has broken a clear house boundary, and calmly enforces a consequence. The response does not always come with raised voices or slammed doors. Sometimes it arrives as a quiet, lethal sidestep, delivered by a child looking past him towards the mother: “I’ll ask my father.” Or worse, it comes from the mother herself, stepping into the hallway to whisper the ultimate domestic veto: “Let’s not make a decision on this until I speak to his father.” With four words, the room undergoes an immediate climate change. The man sitting at the table, the one who pays the rent, fixes the water heater, covers the tuition fees, and buys the groceries is instantly reminded of his true standing in the house. He is not a parent in full standing. He is a financial trustee operating on a temporary visa, easily overruled by the presence of a biological father who may not have set foot in the building for years. If the stepmother’s burden in a reconstituted household is the demand for instant, sacrificial warmth without maternal equity, the stepfather’s burden is an altogether different trap: the expectation of instant, silent authority without clear moral agreement. Society has written a deeply contradictory script for men in second families. On one hand, modern cultural narratives praise the man who steps up to raise children born of another relationship. He is celebrated as a heroic provider,an anchor of stability restoring order to a fractured frame. On the other hand, the moment he asserts genuine household governance demanding accountability, setting curfews, or insisting on respect the tone shifts. He is suddenly viewed with suspicion. An invasive disciplinarian stepping over the line, an outsider intruding upon a private bond between a mother and her flesh and blood. This creates an exhausting limbo for stepfathers. They are trusted to shoulder the heavy financial machinery of fatherhood, but deemed dangerous the moment they claim the moral authority that makes a household function. Yet financial provision alone does not automatically grant total authority over a child, nor should being a stepfather disqualify a man from maintaining an orderly home. A household cannot function well when adults assign financial responsibility without clarifying the boundaries, expectations, and authority that accompany it. To understand why children invoke their biological father, we must look past the adult ego and into the child’s sense of origin. To a child, a biological father even one who is absent, flawed, or deeply unreliable is not just an ex-spouse. He represents their identity, history, and roots. When a stepfather tries to command authority by decree, the child may not hear leadership; they may hear erasure. Defending their biological father’s standing is often the child’s desperate way of defending their own origin story Children do not measure loyalty by school fees paid or bills settled. They may continue to defend a father who has disappointed them repeatedly because they are guarding a relationship they still hope will heal. A stepfather who understands this has a far better chance of building trust than one who treats a child’s loyalty as a personal insult. This dynamic becomes infinitely more fragile when the biological mother acts as an unpredictable buffer rather than a bridge. Driven by lingering guilt over the original family’s collapse, or simply by a protective instinct, mothers in second marriages often step between their new partner and their children. When a mother constantly says, “Let me handle my kids,” or privately reverses agreed rules, she communicates a clear message to her children: His word carries no weight here. The goal is not for a mother to defend a partner when he is unfair, but for both adults to agree on reasonable household rules privately, support each other’s legitimate roles, and refrain from turning discipline into a domestic tug-of-war. The fundamental mistake stepfathers make in response to this tension is attempting to claim authority through volume, economic entitlement, or positional rank. Power derived solely from financial leverage is not authority; it is domestic occupation. The way forward is not to make the stepfather a surrogate patriarch, but to help him find his place as an unshakable, non-competing mentor. This begins when a stepfather stops competing with a ghost. A stepfather who tries to diminish, mock, or replace a biological father will always harden the child’s resistance and turn every house rule into a battle of loyalties. The most powerful stance a man can take is one of quiet composure: respecting the biological father’s irreplaceable historical status without abdicating his own present duty to maintain respect in the home. Alongside this shift, the adults must establish clear, unified boundaries in front of the children. Alignment between partners cannot be a secret kept behind closed doors while remaining invisible at the dinner table. If the adults do not present a clear, shared framework, children will naturally navigate the fault lines to survive. Ultimately, we must redefine what success looks like. A stepfather’s achievement is not measured by whether he is granted the title of “Dad” a heavy, sacred word that belongs to memory and bloodline. His success is measured by whether he becomes a steady, reliable adult presence: a man of clear boundaries, fair judgment, and quiet consistency whose presence enriches a child’s life without forcing them to deny where they came from. A stepfather does not need to defeat a ghost to build a legacy. When he stops fighting for a title he does not need and commits instead to the daily, unglamorous work of being a trustworthy guide, the room stops trembling. His worth is not determined by whether he replaces another man or wins every domestic argument, but by the quiet security he helps create and the honest peace upon which a new home can stand. By Stephanie Shaakaa shaakaastephanie@yahoo.com 08078600871 The post I’ll ask my father, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: American change
items.description: ON the Sunday before Election Day in the US, the Democratic leadership was in uproar. The reason was Israel — though not obviously so. The action took place in Detroit, Michigan, where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed was in a close race against Republican Mike Rogers. Rogers had run a campaign marked by Islamo­phobic attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, portraying him as a security threat and making unfounded allegations of extremist sympathies. In the primary election that decided the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed had defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who had said she “dreamed of Israel” and had benefited from nearly $30 million in spending by pro-Israel lobbies. Despite this, El-Sayed was able to win. Stevens decided that Sunday morning that she would endorse El-Sayed’s opponent, a man she had previously criticised. It was an extraordinary move that drew condemnation from her fellow Democrats and the American left. Appearing at an African-American church alongside Rogers, Stevens said that she just couldn’t support El-Sayed and would, instead, back the Republican. For the 48 hours until the election, Stevens got tons of attention. In an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, she struggled to explain why she had withdrawn support for a candidate she had previously endorsed. Pro-Zionist commentators on the American right were gleeful. Maybe they hoped El-Sayed, who had openly opposed the war against Iran and called Gaza a genocide, would not win. It was a close election, and Stevens might persuade some Black and Jewish voters in Michigan not to vote for the man who would become the first Muslim senator in US history. As we know now, their predictions were wrong. El-Sayed defeated Rogers, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Democrats also won control of both Houses of Congress, while several Muslim candidates, including Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Andre Carson won election or re-election. Democrat victories show voters oppose blanket support for Israel. Of all of them, El-Sayed had been the most plainspoken about the problem with US support for Israel. The particular mastery of his campaign was that it took the very Trumpian rhetoric of ‘America First’ and turned it on its head. El-Sayed argued that politicians who prioritised billions in aid to Israel over domestic needs were putting another country’s interests before those of ordinary Americans. This message resonated with voters all around the country. The issue of whether a politician is ‘America First’ rather than ‘Israel First’ has become part of the political conversation. This is particularly worrisome for establishment Democrats who would compete to demonstrate their love for Israel. The Democratic victories have clearly shown that the party voter wants to end the blanket support for Israel that has long been an American tradition. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, presumptive leaders of the Senate and House, have both said that they do not support sending unending aid to Israel. They know which way the wind is blowing. The biggest evidence of this, however, came from the Republicans — really from the vice president himself. Even as the results were coming in, J.D. Vance took to X and wrote a lengthy post on why his party had lost so abysmally. Vance pointed directly to the war in Iran — which America entered at Israel’s behest — saying it had cost Republicans the election. It was a shocking yet understandable acknowledgment. It made sense for Vance — who is likely to run for president in 2028 — to try and distance himself from Trump right away. Now, he is seeking to ally himself with anti-Israel figures on the American right like Tucker Carlson. Car­lson’s opposition to Israel is pointed in that he said he wou­ld have voted for El-Sayed simply be­­cause he was so fed up with unending support for Israel, which he thought had a harmful influence on America’s politics. Carlson has urged his supporters to understand how American democracy was being turned into a sham by Israeli influence. The America that woke up on Nov 4, 2026, is, therefore, a remarkably different America. Israel’s government has long relied on strong bipartisan support in Washington, and pro-Israel organisations have spent enormous sums to ensure that American politicians will always be in their pocket. Those days are not decisively over. It is likely that when the new lawmakers take office in January, legislation and limits will be pursued on all aid to Israel that could see the amount of military support drastically reduced. America voted for change this week but it is likely that it is Israel — with much reduced US support after January — that will see the greatest change in its circumstances. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. [rafia.zakaria@gmail.com][1] Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

items.title: Scientists turn cancer cells into weapons against tumours
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe What if the chemical produced in abundance by cancer cells could be turned against the cancers? What if, instead of flooding the entire body with powerful drugs in an attempt to destroy a tumour, scientists could persuade cancer cells to manufacture destructive chemicals from within? That possibility is at the centre of an intriguing scientific breakthrough in Japan, where researchers have developed an experimental technique that exploits carbon monoxide produced by cancer cells to generate cancer-killing compounds inside them. The approach turns an unusual feature of cancer biology into a potential therapeutic advantage. Rather than administering an already manufactured toxic drug that circulates through the body and can damage healthy tissues, the researchers have devised a chemical system that produces an anticancer compound inside targeted cancer cells. In laboratory experiments, the technique successfully generated toxic compounds in several cancer cell lines while leaving a noncancerous cell line without detectable production of the same compound. Although still at an early experimental stage, the findings could open a new direction in cancer treatment, particularly in the long-standing search for ways to destroy malignant cells while sparing healthy tissues from the collateral damage associated with conventional chemotherapy. The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI), Japan, was published in Nature Communications. Cancer treatment has long been complicated by a fundamental problem: drugs powerful enough to destroy malignant cells can also injure normal cells. Chemotherapy, for instance, often affects healthy tissues because many anticancer medicines cannot distinguish perfectly between cancerous and noncancerous cells. The resulting damage can produce debilitating side effects, including nausea, fatigue, hair loss and suppression of the immune system. Scientists have consequently been exploring more selective ways of delivering or generating anticancer agents at the precise location where they are needed. Tanaka and colleagues focused on carbon monoxide, a gas commonly recognised for its toxicity but also naturally produced in small quantities in the human body. Their strategy was to deliver a metal-based catalyst into cells and use the available carbon monoxide as the chemical fuel for a reaction that manufactures an anticancer substance. In principle, the reaction would be activated predominantly in cancer cells, where sufficient carbon monoxide is available, rather than in healthy tissues. The research represents part of a developing scientific field known as therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry, which seeks to use chemical reactions inside living organisms to manufacture therapeutic substances where they are needed. items.title: Nigeria is losing $1.6bn yearly to avoidable blindness — Aghaji
items.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru Almost on a daily basis, across Nigeria and much of Africa, millions of people wake up to a world they cannot see clearly. A farmer peeks at his cassava farms for instance, but cannot differentiate the difference between weed and crop. A trader holds her register at arm’s length, guessing at figures she once read at a glance. A child in the back row of a classroom copies from a board that is almost a blur. More often, an old woman needs her grandchild to lead her to the market because the road she walked for over 50 years has become unrecognizable. Those are not statistics. They are the human face of a crisis that Africa has lived with for too long. As Professor Ada Aghaji told a packed hall at the University of Nigeria on October 29, 2026, this is a crisis Africa can no longer afford to ignore. Delivering the institution’s 254th Inaugural Lecture, titled “Let There Be Sight: Building Sustainable Eye Health Systems for All in Africa,” Aghaji, Professor of Ophthalmology and Eye Health Systems, made a simple but very powerful argument: eye health in Africa is not just a medical issue. It is an economic issue. A development issue. A justice issue. And the numbers prove it. According to her, Nigeria loses an estimated $1.6 billion every year in productivity because of vision impairment. Across Africa, the loss is about $9 billion. Globally, it stands at a staggering $410 billion. Behind those figures are livelihoods cut short, schooling interrupted, and families pushed deeper into poverty. Yet, as Aghaji stressed, much of this vision loss can be prevented or treated. A pair of spectacles costing less than a bag of rice. A 15-minute cataract operation. A routine screening at a primary health centre. Why, then, do millions of Africans continue to live with avoidable blindness when the solutions already exist? That was the question at the heart of her lecture. Two Children, Two Worlds Perhaps the most haunting moment of the lecture came not from statistics, but from a story. Aghaji spoke of two children born with congenital rubella syndrome; a condition that can cause cataracts, deafness and other disabilities. One was born in Nigeria. He faced delays, barriers to treatment and rehabilitation, and ended up blind. The other was a Somali refugee child in England. He received timely surgery, spectacles and hearing aids, and with them, a chance to learn, to play, to grow Their medical conditions were similar. Their opportunities were profoundly different. The contrast, Aghaji argued, is the story of Africa’s eye health system in miniature. Medical knowledge alone does not guarantee care. What determines whether a child sees or goes blind is often not the disease, but the system around it: whether there is money to pay, a health worker to detect the problem, a referral that works, a hospital that can be reached. Drawing on her journey from clinical ophthalmology to health-systems research, Aghaji examined the barriers that keep people from care — poverty, too few trained workers, weak referral systems, and eye care that is still not properly integrated into primary health services. “The challenge extends beyond what happens inside an operating theatre,” she said. “It includes the millions who never reach one.” The Economics of Sight If the moral case for eye health is clear, Aghaji made the economic case even clearer According to estimates presented in the lecture, “about $7 billion invested globally in eye health between 2026 and 2030 could generate $199 billion in economic benefits — roughly $28 for every dollar invested. “For Nigeria alone, an estimated $110 million investment could generate about $2.45 billion in benefits over the same period. These are projections, not guaranteed returns. But they point to a truth that policymakers can no longer dismiss: restoring sight pays. When a farmer regains sight, he returns to his farm. When a trader gets the right spectacles, she keeps her business alive. When a child can see clearly, her education improves. When an older person regains independence, a family recovers hours once spent on caregiving; hours that can be used to work, study and earn. The lecture therefore positioned eye health as an important contributor to economic participation, education, household welfare and national productivity. For governments, this strengthens the case for including eye health in national development and health-financing priorities. For industry leaders, it highlights the relationship between vision, workforce productivity and economic performance. Why investment must address the right problems One of the lecture’s central arguments was that increasing investment in eye health is necessary, but the way resources are used is equally important. To illustrate, she presented four hypothetical countries, all with similarly poor cataract surgical coverage, but for very different reasons. One lacked trained surgeons and equipment. Another had services that patients could not afford. A third failed to identify and refer patients who needed surgery. In the fourth, surgery was performed, but the visual outcomes were poor. All four looked the same on paper. The solutions they needed were completely different. More surgeons would not help a patient who cannot afford transport. Free surgery would achieve little if no one ever finds the patient. More operations would mean little if patients do not regain useful vision. The lesson according to Aghaji is that investment must respond to the specific barrier preventing people from receiving effective care. Success, therefore, should not be measured by the number of consultations held, spectacles distributed or operations performed. It should be measured by whether people actually see better. She also harped on equity. This, she noted, must be central, ensuring that women, poorer households, rural populations and people with disabilities are not left behind when services improve. What Rwanda Got Right If Nigeria needs a model, Aghaji pointed to Rwanda. Through sustained government leadership, coordinated partnerships, integration of eye care into primary health services, workforce development and financial protection, Rwanda has steadily expanded access. By training nurses and community health workers and strengthening links between primary care and specialist services, Rwanda has brought eye care closer to communities She however, pointed out that building a system is a continuing process. As more people are identified, demand for treatment increases. Even when surgery is affordable, transport costs and other barriers can still keep patients away. The lesson from Rwanda is not that progress is easy, but that it is possible with leadership, coordination and continuous attention to results. Prof Aghaji’s personal research in Nigeria tells a similar story. In a study of 165 primary health-care facilities across six states, states where allocated primary eye-care budgets were actually released, recorded 16 times as many cataract referrals as states where funds were not released. Health insurance and coordination also made a measurable difference. Money matters. But released money, spent well, matters more. A Shared Responsibility With an estimated 110 million Africans living with vision loss, the scale of the challenge is far beyond what ophthalmologists and specialist hospitals alone can handle, according to Aghaji. She called for eye care to be integrated into primary health care, for referral systems to be strengthened, for financial protection to be improved, and for investment to be judged by measurable improvements in people’s lives. Government leadership, according to her, must provide the foundation. But the private sector, professional associations, civil society and development partners all have a role. For businesses, there are opportunities in workforce eye-health programmes, affordable spectacles, technological innovation and investment in service delivery. For development partners, the challenge is to support national priorities and help build systems that can sustain progress long after a project ends. The timing of the lecture could not be more significant. As the global eye-health community gathers for the 2026 Global Summit for Eye Health in Antigua and Barbuda, new investments offer an opportunity to accelerate progress. But their ultimate value, Aghaji argued, will be judged not by pledges made, but by improvements in effective coverage, visual outcomes and equity. Let There Be Sight In the end, Aghaji’s lecture returned to where it began: people. The consequences of poor vision extend beyond hospitals into classrooms, workplaces, households and national economies. Conversely, restoring and protecting sight can expand opportunities for education, employment, independence and dignity. Africa cannot achieve its full prosperity, she argued, while millions of its people remain unnecessarily blind or visually impaired The challenge, therefore, is not simply to increase eye-care expenditure, but to build sustainable systems that connect people to effective services, address the barriers they face and deliver outcomes that matter For governments, industry leaders and development partners, the opportunity is to turn investment into restored sight, improved livelihoods and greater economic participation That was the vision at the heart of the University of Nigeria’s 254th Inaugural Lecture: Let There Be Sight; not as a privilege for a few, but as an opportunity for all Africans. items.title: The debt burden
items.description: PAKISTAN’S external debt has nearly doubled in a decade — from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025 — according to a new World Bank report. Public and publicly guaranteed debt accounts for $107.1bn of the total, private debt for $17.6bn, and short-term borrowing for $10.45bn. China is the largest single creditor with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank. The rise itself is not surprising but the pace is striking. Much of this borrowing went towards plugging external financing gaps, propping up reserves, and repaying older loans to keep the economy running. The debt spike describes an economy that invests, produces and earns too little to service what it owes. Debt has become the main constraint on our fiscal and economic prospects. Servicing debt eats up meagre financial resources, which should be expanding productive capacity for exports, and makes faster growth harder to reach. That leads to more borrowing. The government borrows to cover consumption, budget deficits, and external payments — not to build anything that pays for itself. Development spending is usually the first thing to be cut, and growth has crawled along at 2.7pc in recent years. There is nothing wrong with borrowing. Developing economies need foreign capital for infrastructure, energy, technology, and industry. The trouble starts when loans do not raise domestic productivity or lift exports. Successive governments have failed to tell apart borrowing that builds capacity from borrowing that only buys time. Pakistan’s recurring balance-of-payments crisis underscores this fact. The country’s exports are weak, the production base is narrow, investment is low, and fiscal deficits refuse to go away. So, the economy keeps relying on foreign and domestic loans. Remittances, rollovers by friendly countries, and one IMF programme after another may have staved off immediate default, but none of them has addressed the underlying problem. It does not matter much if the country can raise another loan or defer another repayment. What matters is whether the country can generate enough growth, tax revenue, and foreign exchange to meet its obligations without sacrificing its development. The situation calls for a credible, short- to long-term strategy to invest in projects that raise productivity, exports, and foreign exchange earnings. The strategy must be accompanied by wider reforms aimed at expansion of the tax base, more productive public spending, and lower costs of doing business. Exporters need energy that is reliable and competitively priced, policies they can predict, and access to modern technology. Without these, even fresh foreign investment and cheaper credit will yield little value, growth will remain anaemic, children stunted, and communities without basic services such as clean drinking water. And debt will continue to constrain the country’s economic sovereignty and prosperity. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026
