items.title: A Chief of Staff Who ‘Will Crack Skulls’
items.description: I n the days before MAGA’s midterm disaster , President Trump began complaining about his presidency. He felt stuck. The war in Iran wouldn’t end. Inflation wouldn’t subside. Little was going his way. But in the president’s mind, there was one exception: “Stephen is the only one who gets stuff done,” Trump repeatedly griped, a person close to the White House told us. “I need more people who get stuff done.” Stephen Miller, one of the president’s hardest-charging and longest-serving aides, had managed to maintain Trump’s trust, even though he is the architect of the administration’s sweeping mass-deportation campaign that many in the GOP blame, in part, for the Republicans’ historic wipeout this week. Today, Trump announced that Miller would replace Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, completing his decade-long journey from congressional staffer to the most powerful aide in Washington. Where Wiles served as something of a guardrail—making sure Trump was fully briefed and that he understood the risks and pitfalls of any decision—Miller has played the role of an accelerant for a president who already has rash tendencies. One issue on which Wiles and Miller seem to diverge: how to force journalists to reveal their sources in the government. Trump has pushed the Department of Justice to pursue criminal-leak investigations on national-security grounds, and there have been discussions in the White House and at DOJ about various tactics they could use—including arrests—as part of those efforts, according to three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said that Wiles had pushed back. Miller, though, was in favor and insisted that it wouldn’t take long for journalists to give up their sources, they told us. A DOJ spokesperson told us via text that “this is absolutely false” but declined to elaborate. A White House spokesperson told us in a statement that unauthorized leaks will “NEVER be tolerated” and those responsible “must be held accountable.” One person familiar with Trump’s decision to elevate Miller told us that the president wants somebody who “will crack skulls,” adding that Trump “doesn’t want to be reined in.” Another described Miller as someone with significant Capitol Hill experience who could manage the coming clashes with Democrats. White House officials have held high-level conversations in recent days, including with Miller, about areas where they can work with Democrats. But another person familiar with Trump’s thinking said there was no need for a chief of staff who could work the Hill to pass legislation, because nothing was going to get done. “The next two years are going to be nonstop political warfare,” this person told us—and Miller can be the face of that fight. This account of Wiles’s ouster and Miller’s ascent is based on interviews with six people familiar with the situation, all of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. Inside the White House, officials understood that Trump would never blame himself for Republican midterm losses, and the West Wing has spent the past few days wondering whom Trump would punish. When The New York Times published a story about the defeat—with verbatim leaks of Trump’s top political team joking ahead of the election about how grim it all looked—Wiles found herself taking heat from the president. Two people familiar with the matter told us that Trump felt that the story, which featured Wiles’s allies seeming to laugh at Republican failure, was a betrayal, and he expressed his displeasure to her. Trump met with Wiles on Wednesday, and she volunteered to resign, but no decision was made. By yesterday, Wiles was telling her deputies that she had a resignation letter ready and was prepared to leave. She had spent months running the White House while undergoing treatment for breast cancer, and has described herself as “tired” to colleagues. The president announced her departure today after the Times reached out to the White House about her rumored exit. Wiles did not view her role as a roadblock to Trump’s most extreme impulses. On many of the White House’s most consequential decisions, she did not directly weigh in. During the debate over the Iran war, for instance, advisers said, she focused on making sure that Trump was fully briefed on the risks, although others in the White House described her as concerned. Her replacement, who takes over on Monday, is known both for his effectiveness and his hard-line views. Miller appeared with Trump tonight at an event at Mar-a-Lago and said: “I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.” M iller has been with Trump from the beginning. He was an aide to Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who became the first senator to endorse Trump’s 2016 campaign. Before long, Miller was designing policy proposals—particularly those that reflected his hard-line immigration views—and sometimes appearing as a fiery warm-up act at Trump’s rallies. He co-authored the first term’s so-called Muslim ban, became known for his high-volume and belligerent TV interviews defending Trump, and was one of the few staffers to navigate the often-competing power centers in the dysfunctional West Wing. (In both terms, he has remained well liked by colleagues, who appreciate his straightforwardness and dry sense of humor.) Miller oversaw the writing of the speech that Trump delivered from the Ellipse on January 6, 2021, ahead of the Capitol insurrection, and his influence only grew during Trump’s four years out of power. Miller used that time to help write Project 2025, a playbook for Trump’s return to the White House that included a broad expansion of executive power. At the core of Miller’s agenda was a sweeping deportation program. Masked ICE agents detained people in quiet neighborhoods and Home Depot parking lots, while Miller demanded that dramatic deportation quotas be met. Americans, polling showed, began to view the tactics as extreme, particularly after the killing of two Americans in Minneapolis early this year. Trump’s political team has privately blamed Miller’s aggressive immigration policy in part for the defeat on Tuesday , because violent ICE clashes and ethnic profiling on the streets have alienated both Latino voters and moderate independents. Miller has already been operating as a de facto chief of staff for the Department of Homeland Security and the president’s mass-deportation campaign. He hosts conference calls six days a week with top officials from agencies across the government who are enlisted to help ICE with the crackdown. Officials who participate in the calls say that Miller often berates staff who disappoint him or lack the information he wants. The White House press office promised in a statement tonight that Miller “will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Recently, Trump had begun telling people close to him that he was considering changing his immigration emphasis, recognizing that although voters supported his tough border-security stance, ICE’s brutal approach to rounding up undocumented immigrants, including those who are not criminals, was provoking a backlash. Trump had begun to hear from business owners about their employees being deported, along with the nannies and tutors of friends, and he was open to pivoting. Miller, as his chief of staff, will now directly oversee the policy debate, a shift from his role as the resident immigration hawk in the White House. S ince 2021, Wiles has been responsible for building the political campaign—and, later, the White House structure—around Trump. After January 6, at a time when most Republicans were keeping their distance from Trump, she offered him a core group of advisers, bringing in the veteran campaign strategist Chris LaCivita to help run the 2024 campaign, along with the strategists Taylor Budowich and James Blair , operatives with Florida political experience who would go on to senior roles in the White House. (Miller during this period operated outside the president’s inner circle, from a new legal operation focused on pursuing MAGA priorities.) Inside the White House, she was known for her calm and organization, and her ability to do what no other chief of staff to Trump had ever done: Guide the sometimes-mercurial president, regularly stepping in to try to prevent risky decisions, while at the same time allowing him to run his presidency on his own terms. Wiles was well liked by many Republicans who appreciated the degree of levelheadedness she brought to the West Wing. She grew up as the daughter of an alcoholic, the football play-by-play caller Pat Summerall. Trump does not drink, but in an interview with Vanity Fair in 2025, Wiles said there were similarities between her father and the president, who she said had an “alcoholic’s personality,” and that had helped her in the job. But she slowed down this year. In March, shortly after the conflict with Iran began, she was diagnosed with breast cancer, forcing her to spend much of the campaign season juggling one of the most demanding jobs in government with regular chemotherapy appointments. She described the ordeal as “ brutal and unrelenting ,” and said that she sometimes had to fight to get out of bed. Trump’s poll numbers collapsed, largely because of high prices fueled by the war and his haphazard tariffs program. Wiles had built a team of loyalists—to both her and the president—in the White House and steered the West Wing to a series of successes last year, including passing its signature piece of legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. At the start of the term, White House advisers, including Wiles, took steps to turn the broad coalition that had elected Trump into regular Republican voters. Wiles never stopped the president from relying on other advisers as well—both in and outside the administration. In recent weeks, some of those advisers became more crucial. Corey Lewandowski, who clashed with Wiles during the 2024 campaign, shared a social-media post after the election blaming Republican “political consultants” for giving “really bad advice.” And just hours before Trump announced Wiles’s departure, a former deputy to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , Calley Means, appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast and accused the chief of staff of standing in the way of the Make America Healthy Again agenda by siding with pesticide, tobacco, and food-industry concerns during policy debates. [ Read: The White House’s MAHA gatekeeper ] Other powerful forces in Trump’s orbit also targeted Wiles. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte —who recently generated a minor scandal by spilling cola on the carpet of Trump’s new Air Force One, two people told us—had complained that she was holding Trump back. (Pulte has publicly praised Wiles.) And Miller’s wife, Katie, a former aide in the White House and to Elon Musk who is an influential voice in MAGA circles, began to push for her husband’s ascension. Stephen Miller, his supporters say, is the right person to steer the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Despite the scale of this week’s Democratic victory, the president has rarely reached across the aisle in the past. In recent days, he made his feelings known with a new red hat displayed on the Resolute Desk. It was emblazoned with a single word: VETO . Nick Miroff contributed to this report.

items.title: Ghana loses $6.5bn in potential mining revenue – IFS
items.description: The country loses an estimated $6.56 billion in potential revenue from the mining sector every year due to the government’s limited participation in mineral extraction, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has revealed. The institute explained that the country could have generated that additional money from mining in 2025 if its revenue generation from the sector had matched Botswana’s performance due to its active involvement in the sector. The Executive Director of the IFS, Dr Said Boakye, who made this known at a policy briefing on low government revenue mobilisation in Accra yesterday, said the situation reflected the country’s inability to maximise returns from its considerable mineral resources, and, therefore, asked the authorities to use the upcoming 2027 Budget to correct the leakage. Dr Boakye further identified revenue leakages, including tax evasion, underreporting, tax avoidance and collusion involving revenue administrators, as major factors undermining domestic revenue mobilisation. He cited revelations by the Commissioner-General of the Ghana Revenue Authority, Anthony Sarpong, in April 2026 that the country had lost more than GH¢11 billion in revenue at its ports through incorrect declarations involving the country of origin, classification and valuation of imported goods. He said the low government revenue mobilisation had constrained the country’s ability to finance development. Dr Boakye added that the country’s total revenue and grants-to-GDP ratio stood at 15.7 per cent in 2022, against the average of 20.1 per cent for 25 sub-Saharan African countries examined in the IFS report. The institute estimated that Ghana would have collected GH¢288.26 billion in total revenue and grants in 2025 if its revenue-to-GDP ratio had matched the sub-Saharan African average, compared with the actual collection of GH¢224.88 billion. Poor performance The figure, he said, placed Ghana 18th among the 25 countries, highlighting the country’s relatively poor performance compared with its regional peers. Comparing the systems in Ghana to Botswana’s, for instance, he said the southern African country generated $13.4 billion in value added from mining in 2025, while Ghana’s revenue from the sector amounted to only $1.6 billion, representing 11.9 per cent of the sector’s value. He said if it had generated mining revenue at Botswana’s average rate of 60.9 per cent, the government would have earned $8.16 billion instead of the $1.6 billion collected. Dr Boakye attributed Botswana’s stronger performance to the government’s active involvement in the mining sector through partnerships with private companies. He explained that such arrangements enabled Botswana to benefit from corporate income taxes, dividends and royalties, while gaining better insight into the operations and profitability of mining companies. “The government of Botswana does not only earn large corporate income tax revenue from mining because it has an insider knowledge of mining operations and profitability, it earns even larger revenue from dividend payments and royalties,” he said. He contrasted the arrangement with Ghana’s concession-based system, under which private companies largely undertake mineral extraction, leaving the government with limited access to information about their operations and profitability. Dr Boakye said the revenue shortfall had serious implications for public investment and the country’s debt situation. “The low government revenue mobilisation usually leads to shortage of money to fund the government’s developmental projects, making it resort to borrowing. This has led to frequent large debt build-ups, high debt service costs, and fiscal or debt crisis,” he stated. Tax exemptions Dr Boakye further identified excessive tax exemptions granted to businesses as another factor contributing to the country’s weak revenue performance. The report cited incentives under the Free Zones regime and the automotive industry development policy, which offered businesses tax holidays, import duty exemptions and other fiscal concessions. Dr Boakye said the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre’s incentives inventory lists 31 income tax, customs and financial incentive packages available to businesses across various sectors. Recommendation To address the challenges, Dr Boakye recommended greater government participation in the extractive sector through direct investment and partnerships with private companies. He also proposed production-sharing agreements as an alternative to the existing concession arrangements, saying such agreements would provide the government with better returns from the exploitation of the country’s natural resources. He further called for an intensified fight against corruption within tax and non-tax revenue collection agencies, alongside a review of existing tax incentive packages. Dr Boakye urged the government to discontinue exemptions which did not make economic sense in relation to the revenue being forfeited, and to rely more on improvements in the macroeconomic and political environment to attract investment.

items.title: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate?
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike The African Democratic Congress (ADC) was meant to be the meeting point of opposition forces determined to challenge President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Instead, the party has become the battleground for a struggle that could undo the coalition it was expected to accommodate. Read Also: Court sacks Mark-led ADC exco, voids Atiku’s candidacy Barely 24 hours after former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar took his presidential campaign to Sokoto, a Federal High Court judgment delivered by Justice Peter Lifu threw the party into fresh uncertainty, nullifying the David Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including the process that produced Atiku as presidential candidate. For Mark and his allies, it was a setback at a critical moment. For Nafiu Bala Gombe, who challenged the leadership transition, it was a victory in a battle he had refused to abandon. For Atiku, it was a reminder that the platform on which he hopes to return to Aso Rock may not be entirely within his control. With the Mark faction preparing to appeal, attention is shifting to the appellate courts. Whatever the eventual outcome, the political fortunes of some of the coalition’s most prominent figures are at stake. How it all began The dispute began when former ADC National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu, facilitated a leadership transition that brought Mark and former Osun State Governor, Rauf Aregbesola, into the party as National Chairman and National Secretary respectively. The arrangement offered opposition politicians an existing political structure around which to build a challenge to the APC. But Gombe, a former Deputy National Chairman, North, objected, arguing that the party’s constitution provided a succession procedure that was not followed. His challenge produced Justice Lifu’s November 5 judgment. The Mark faction, however, insists that the leadership question had already been examined by the court. It points to the July 2, 2026, judgment of Justice Musa Liman in a separate suit instituted by House of Representatives member Leke Abejide. Justice Liman upheld preliminary objections, including lack of jurisdiction, standing and failure to exhaust internal party remedies. He also made findings favourable to the defendants concerning the leadership transition The Mark camp argues that a court of coordinate jurisdiction cannot overturn another court’s decision. However, the different plaintiffs and the precise issues and reliefs sought in the two cases make the legal relationship between the judgments a matter requiring highest judicial determination. The Supreme Court had intervened on April 30, setting aside an earlier status quo ante bellum order and directing an expedited hearing at the Federal High Court. It did not decide who was entitled to lead the ADC While Mark’s camp rejects the latest judgment, Gombe has celebrated it as a victory for constitutional governance. “Political parties are not above their own constitutions, and the Electoral Act is not a mere suggestion,” he declared. If Gombe wins at S-Court, where does Atiku go? A final Supreme Court victory for Gombe could leave Atiku facing a difficult political calculation. If the court upholds the nullification of the Mark-led leadership and its consequential decisions, the former Vice-President’s presidential nomination could become legally untenable. His political influence would remain, but finding another viable platform at this stage would be difficult. Atiku has made clear that he intends to fight the judgment. “My roots are in Northern Nigeria, but my candidacy belongs to all Nigerians. There is a difference between being from the North and being a candidate only for the North,” he said in a statement by his campaign spokesman, Phrank Shaibu. A Gombe victory at the apex court would also cost Mark and Aregbesola their positions and potentially undermine the machinery through which the coalition intends to contest the elections. The consequences could extend to governorship, Senate, House of Representatives and State Assembly candidates whose nominations were made under the disputed leadership. Their electoral ambitions could be affected if the final orders invalidate those nominations. For Gombe, however, winning the chairmanship would not automatically mean inheriting the coalition’s political networks, resources and prominent figures. He would have to decide whether to accommodate the politicians who joined under Mark or risk a party weakened by their departure. Nwosu would equally face renewed questions about the leadership transition he facilitated, although a judgment against Mark’s structure would not automatically establish personal wrongdoing on his part. If Mark wins at S-Court, Gombe faces another choice A final victory for Mark would preserve the coalition’s leadership structure, strengthen the position of existing ADC candidates and remove the immediate legal threat to Atiku’s ticket. Aregbesola would retain his position, while Atiku could concentrate on his campaign rather than spend valuable time defending his political platform. Rotimi Amaechi, his presidential running mate, and other candidates would also have greater certainty over their nominations. Gombe, meanwhile, would have to decide whether to remain in the party, accept the coalition’s leadership or seek another political arrangement. His influence would depend on the support he retains among the ADC’s original membership. But a Mark victory would not automatically end the internal struggle. The coalition brings together politicians with different ambitions and constituencies. Their common opposition to Tinubu does not mean they agree on the distribution of party offices, influence and political opportunities. Mark would still have to demonstrate that the ADC can function as a political party rather than an alliance held together principally by the desire to challenge the APC. The election clock is ticking The electoral timetable makes the dispute particularly consequential. INEC has scheduled the presidential and National Assembly elections for January 16, 2027, and governorship and State Assembly elections for February 6. The deadlines for party primaries and replacement of presidential candidates have passed. Consequently, a Gombe victory would not automatically give the recognised leadership an opportunity to conduct fresh primaries and nominate new candidates. Whether existing nominations survive would depend on the final appellate orders, their scope and the applicable electoral provisions. For thousands of candidates, the dispute is no longer simply an argument between political heavyweights in Abuja. It is about whether their names will remain on the ballot after months of campaigning. The ADC has accused the APC of exploiting the crisis to weaken the opposition. The ruling party has denied involvement, describing the matter as an internal ADC dispute. Those allegations remain contested. Ultimately, the Supreme Court may determine who legally controls the ADC, but it cannot guarantee that the victorious faction will retain the loyalty of the coalition. If Gombe wins, he could secure the party but struggle to retain the coalition. If Mark wins, he could preserve the coalition’s platform but still face the task of reconciling an aggrieved original membership. For Atiku, the immediate question is whether his presidential ambition can survive the loss of its chosen platform. items.title: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’
items.description: •Says, I share your pain, we’re out of dark tunnel •Knocks Atiku, Obi in Uyo, approves Ibom Deep Sea Port •Bus conveying women to welcome President crashes By Egufe Yafugborhi UYO — PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu yesterday promised a better future for Nigerians even as he took a swipe at former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), declaring that they lacked the leadership qualities to govern Nigeria. Read Also: 2027: Obi couldn’t confront Anambra’s erosion, he lacks leadership traits — Tinubu Tinubu, presidential candidate of the All Progressives Congress, APC, spoke during his visit to Akwa Ibom State, where he urged voters to support his administration and Governor Umo Eno, insisting that continuity was necessary to sustain development. His visit, however, was overshadowed by a road crash involving an Akwa Ibom State Transport Corporation (AKTC) bus conveying women to welcome him, in which one person was feared dead and several others sustained serious injuries. The accident occurred along Oron Road, Uyo, when the bus, reportedly heading towards the airport, collided with a security Hilux van. Both vehicles were badly damaged. Addressing supporters at the rally, Tinubu described his visit as a homecoming, recalling his professional connection with Akwa Ibom through his early employment with Mobil Oil. “It’s like a homecoming for me. I remember having cut my teeth with Deloitte, the greatest accounting firm in America. I expressed the desire to come home. Mobil Oil recruited me. “Part of the first assignment I was given was to audit the operations of Mobil in Eket. We used to go by boat to Ibono Terminal at that time. Akwa Ibom and I have been united ever since then. Till now, they decided that we are going to keep good company,” he said. The President urged the electorate, particularly young people, to obtain their Permanent Voter Card (PVCs), describing it as their most potent instrument for determining the country’s political future. “To you, the youth, do you have your PVC? Show me your hand if you have your PVC. To me, that is your sword. That is the weapon you need to defeat tyranny, to defeat those who deceive, those who don’t appreciate the value of a growing economy and the value of promising prosperity. “The weapon you have is the PVC. I don’t have to enumerate what I’ve done for you. I’ve committed my last years to struggling for democracy, freedom, authenticity, development and progress,” Tinubu said. He urged the people to support continuity, arguing that his administration had delivered improvements in education and other sectors. “Have you seen development or not? You have seen progress. Your university is no longer on strike. There’s economic value being added to your life,” he told the crowd. Tinubu then promised a better future through infrastructure development, education, skills acquisition and employment opportunities. “I’m begging you for the sake of your future. I promise you a better future; I promise you development; I promise you education; I promise you skill development; I promise you jobs. We are going to plant a lot of economic trees. There’s no reason why Akwa Ibom cannot use the value of palm trees,” he added. Defends his economic policies He described the January 16, 2027 election as consequential, saying it would determine the country’s direction. He also defended his economic policies saying his administration had moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse. According to him, “This coming election, on January 16th is a consequential election. It will define the direction of this country. When I took over, 27 governors out of 36 of this country were unable to pay salary, not to talk of pension, and gratuity. Today I can say that we are out of that tunnel. And I can beat my chest to say we are out of the despair, the dark tunnel of uncertainty and the calamity of a possible bankruptcy. By now if we didn’t take over, if we didn’t do what we did, we will be using the wheelbarrows to move our naira about because it will have become valueless.” Acknowledging the hardship associated with his economic reforms, he added: “It was difficult; it was hard. It was hard for me, too. I don’t know the pain of the market, but I share your pain. I share your difficulty. He also defended the student loan programme, saying it was designed to remove the burden of tuition fees from parents and widen access to education. “We’re taking education as the greatest weapon against poverty and creating opportunity for those who are still coming behind. From today on, as we are fighting corruption, any recovered corruption proceeds would be channelled into the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) Tinubu further insisted that Nigeria would not return to fuel subsidy, using a biblical analogy of Moses and the Israelites crossing the Red Sea to argue that the country must move forward rather than return to its previous economic policies. Knocks Obi, Atiku Taking a direct swipe at Obi, the NDC presidential candidate, Tinubu said: “Obi ran away from erosion in Anambra and he will now want to be president? President of where?” He also criticised Atiku over his political movements, questioning his ability to manage a political party and lead the country. “Immediately a little inclination came that they were going to challenge leadership, he ran away. He abandoned the party. He now belongs to another party, and he’s looking for the presidency? Will you give such a person opportunity who has no leadership quality, no sense of responsibility?” he asked. Approves deep sea port A major highlight of the rally was Tinubu’s response to Governor Eno’s appeal for Federal Government approval of the Ibom Deep Sea Port. Responding to the request, the President declared: “On behalf of the people and leadership of Akwa Ibom, the governor requested for Ibom Deep Sea Port. It’s approved.” The declaration drew loud cheers from supporters, who repeatedly chanted: “Thank you, President! Thank you, President! Thank you, President!” Tinubu said the project would generate economic value and accelerate development in the state. “Ibom Deep Sea Port will bring associated economic value and economic development,” he said. He also praised Eno for what he described as his commitment to addressing erosion and promoting development, urging the people to support the governor. “Governor Eno confronted the erosion in Akwa Ibom, and it’s working for you. It’s stable. They lack the leadership character and traits,” he said in an apparent reference to his political opponents. Praises Eno, defends reforms At a reception held in his honour at Ibom Palm Resort, Tinubu praised Eno, describing the resort as evidence of purposeful leadership and the possibility of reclaiming environmentally degraded land for productive use. “We are standing on a resort to the glory of God, which is a product of 73 acres of land of gully erosion, reclaimed, surrounded with a good, romantic, artificial lake, demonstrating a serious vision that is achievable when honest people are working for their homes,” he said. Auto crash Meanwhile, during the President’s visit there was a crash involving the AKTC bus conveying women mobilised to join supporters welcoming him. The bus reportedly collided with a security Hilux van along Oron Road as the women headed towards the airport. Eyewitnesses said one person was feared dead, while several others sustained serious injuries and required emergency assistance. Footage of the aftermath shared by Nsikakabasi Akpan showed early responders and other persons struggling to evacuate injured occupants from the wreckage. Akpan described the incident as a collision involving a bus conveying women to the airport to receive the President and a security vehicle. Confirming the accident, Paul James, Public Relations Officer, Road Safety Operations, Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Akwa Ibom State Command, said the command had dispatched a response team to the scene. James, however, said the command was yet to establish the extent of casualties and the circumstances surrounding the collision as of the time of filing this report. items.title: Nouvelles manifestations samedi en France, avant des annonces du gouvernement
items.description: La colère sociale ne retombe pas en France. De nouvelles manifestations sont prévues samedi sous haute sécurité pour le quatrième week-end consécutif, avec pour épicentre Paris où des gilets jaunes entendent s'approcher des lieux de pouvoir, deux jours après une mobilisation nationale de grande ampleur à l'appel des syndicats. Entre 575.000 personnes, selon les autorités, et 1,6 million, selon le syndicat CGT, ont défilé jeudi dans toute la France pour réclamer une hausse de leur pouvoir d'achat. La nouvelle mobilisation de samedi vise à maintenir la pression deux jours avant une conférence sociale avec les syndicats et le patronat français convoquée par le gouvernement lundi matin et des rencontres avec les organisations lycéennes et étudiantes l'après-midi. Dans un courrier envoyé vendredi aux partenaires sociaux, le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu, confronté à un automne social très chaud, assure « (entendre) les attentes exprimées sur les salaires et le pouvoir d’achat » et les « inquiétudes » des employeurs. Cette conférence « permettra de présenter les réponses concrètes aux attentes des Français », affirme-t-il. L'intersyndicale de jeunesse et des unions syndicales régionales appellent à manifester samedi « contre la vie chère et pour la jeunesse » au sein d'un cortège autorisé, sur le même tracé que jeudi, dans Paris entre la place de la République à celle de la Nation. La coordination des gilets jaunes a elle décidé de faire cavalier seul, marquant clairement ses distances avec les syndicats. items.title: CBN updates guidelines for stablecoins operation
items.description: •Sets N15bn capital requirement By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Central Bank of Nigeria has issued guidelines for virtual asset providers in the country, setting minimum capital requirement of N10 billion and N15 billion for Classes 1 and 2 issuers, respectively. This was contained in a circular with reference number PSP/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, date November 5, 2026 and signed by the Director of Payments Systems Policy, Mr. Musa Jimoh. According to the bank, “A Class 1 Licensed Issuer shall maintain paid-up capital of N10 billion Naira or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. Class 2 Licensed Issuer shall maintain minimum paid-up capital of N15 billion or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. “Both classes shall comply with the capital deposit and corresponding evidence and supplementary requirements in Section 17. There is no offshore issuer exemption from incorporation, licensing or capital.” Class 2 stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against foreign currencies, including the US dollar, while Class 1 refers to issuers of naira-referenced stablecoins. CBN said the emergence of virtual assets, stablecoins, and tokenised payment instruments “presents significant opportunities for innovation in payments, remittances, settlement, and digital commerce,” but that, “their growing adoption also introduces risks relating to financial stability, monetary policy, consumer protection, illicit finance, operational resilience, and foreign exchange management.” It added that the guidelines were issued pursuant to its statutory mandate to promote monetary and financial stability and regulate Nigeria’s payments system. “These Guidelines establish a risk-based framework for the licensing, regulation, supervision, and oversight of Non-Security Virtual Assets, including stablecoins, Deposit Money Tokens (DMTs), and related Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs). “These Guidelines seek to support responsible innovation while safeguarding the integrity, stability, and efficiency of the Nigerian financial system. “These Guidelines also seek to provide regulatory requirements relating to governance, prudential standards, consumer protection, operational resilience, AML/CFT/CPF compliance, and reporting obligations for entities and persons engaged in regulated non-security virtual asset activities within or involving Nigeria,” the bank explained. The CBN’s updated framework outlines clear boundaries for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), with a sharp focus on foreign exchange liquidity, consumer protection, and peer-to-peer (P2P) trading identity protocols. Curbing money laundering The guidelines place great responsibilities on issuers to ensure that their activities do not aid money laundering or terrorism financing, as they are required to provide detailed data on their customers. To avert it from being used for money laundering on terrorism financing, the CBN said “A provider shall maintain criteria, approved by its board and notified to the Bank, for identifying a customer that buys, sells or exchanges Regulated Tokens on the Person-to-Person (P2P) Service as a business, having regard to transaction volume, frequency, number of counterparties and advertising of rates. “The provider shall apply enhanced due diligence and transaction limits to such customer and report the customer to the Bank under Section 10.8. Such identification shall not constitute authorisation to conduct a regulated activity. A customer conducting an activity requiring authorisation shall obtain the applicable licence or authorisation, cease the activity, or operate as an agent of the provider under Section 21, as the Bank may direct.” Among others, the objectives, the apex bank said were to: establish a comprehensive, risk-based regulatory framework governing the issuance, distribution, conversion, custody, transfer, redemption and settlement of Non-Security Virtual Assets, including stablecoins and Deposit Money Tokens; preserve the effectiveness of the Bank’s monetary policy instruments and its capacity to monitor and manage capital flows and foreign exchange dynamics; and protect holders and consumers from issuer insolvency, reserve or backing mismanagement, redemption denial, fraud and other conduct risks; safeguard the stability and integrity of the Nigerian financial system. The regulations applied to Naira-Referenced Stablecoins; Foreign Currency-Referenced Stablecoins; Deposit Money Tokens (DMTs); Other Designated Tokens determined by the CBN to fall within its mandate over payments, settlement, foreign exchange, banking or financial stability; and any other token designated by the bank as a Regulated Token under these Guidelines. items.title: January 2027: Tinubu’s achilles heel, by Muyiwa Adetiba
items.description: The world witnessed a blue wave as the Democrats swept the recently concluded mid-term elections in the United States. Many contested areas had a touch of blue. Even areas that had always been crimson turned deep purple as Democrats made significant inroads into republican comfort zones. Many Republican Congressmen ended up winning in these areas by the skin of their teeth. It was the worse rout in years, some say decades. To be fair, the signs were always there that Republicans would drop seats. Incumbents always do traditionally. And this incumbent had done little to sway tradition. If anything, he exacerbated it. Affordability was an issue in the US – as it still is in many parts of the world – before President Trump ascended the most powerful seat in the world. It was, along immigration, one of the things he promised to tackle. Instead, he toyed with it, calling it fake and a ruse for Democrats to gain attention. But affordability was a reality that stared an average American in the face every time they visited the stores. It was neither red nor blue. The negative rating at the polls for the President showed they were not amused. Something needed to be done to stem the poor rating when the mid-term elections were less than a year away. So the man who loves to be loved, the deal maker who loves quick fixes, the closet dictator who loves a show of power invaded Iran and killed – for want of a milder word – all their leaders in one fell swoop. He rode roughshod into a territory his predecessors had feared to tread. He thought it would all be over in weeks and his rating would get a lift. He thought he would emerge as a knight in shining armor – Americans love a war hero. But Iran is no Venezuela. This ill-advised war of choice is in its ninth month with no end in sight. Only casualties. Only consequences. One of the consequences is the cost of fuel. And by the time he embarked on his frenzied campaign tour to try to stave the threatening blue wave, it was too little, too late. Besides, he was seen as the problem by many and it is not often that the problem becomes the solution. The Iran war has destabilized the Middle-East which is the world’s energy belt. The consequence of that has reverberated all over the world and has become a tipping point to countries which are already contending with affordability issues. The recent riots in Europe and Latin America are examples of discontents caused by a rising cost of living. The result of the recent mid-term election in the US is, in many ways, a consequence of that as well. It is a bad time to seek a re-election as the Israeli Prime Minister and many world leaders have found out. Nigeria goes to the poll in just about two months. Our incumbent is in a pole position unlike many incumbents who are fighting for electoral survival in many parts of the world as we speak. There are ostensibly, many reasons for this. The main one is that the opposition is not united. Because of this, it is like broomsticks that are easily broken when they refuse to come together to make a broom. It is fighting with flaying hands like an agitated wife fighting a sturdy husband. The second main reason is that our elections are hardly issue based. There are many primordial factors affecting the outcome of elections. The opposition, disunited and disoriented, is playing up these age-old primordial factors. Instead of focusing on the cost of living crisis, it is focused on Tinubu. ‘It’s the economy, stupid’ said Bill Clinton many moons ago when he was challenging an incumbent. But this opposition doesn’t get that. Instead, it is Tinubu this, Tinubu that. It as if the issues are personal. Or should even be personal. The opposition should learn a thing or two from the Democrats who were laser focused on the economy. The incumbent on the other hand is street smart. He is like a chess player who knows the weaknesses of his opponent. He also has the resources financially and coercively, to sway the polls in his favor. And as long as opposition continues to play the game along tribal, ‘emilokan’ lines, as long as solutions to issues that affect the working class are not focused on, the incumbent would have the day come January 16. The so called ‘obidients’ for example, are not likely to win more independent souls with their aggressive and abusive approach to dissent. If your principal has some strengths – and he does – then articulate them. If he has antecedents in words and deeds that can promote a more united and more economically buoyant country, then articulate them. Stop attacking dissent. It is not the best way to win new friends. The President’s Achilles heel in this election is the economy. Not necessarily the fundamentals which he had tried to correct through the reforms and on which many think he has scored a pass mark – at least, they have stabilized the economy. But in the attendant fall-out from the reforms which in his haste and hubris, he failed to correctly address. I use the words ‘haste’ and ‘hubris’ advisedly. No serious economist or public commentator would question the need for the reforms. The reforms were long overdue because we were running a dysfunctional economy. But the way they were handled can easily turn a hero into a villain. A bit of sensitivity, a bit of time to cross the ‘Ts’ and dot the ‘I’ could have made a difference. A more empathetic approach to the suffering of the people could have made a difference. That is haste that could have been better managed. Many Nigerians have dropped into the poverty zone. The US led war against Iran has not helped matters. Almost all Nigerians have received severe knocks on their quality of life. I say almost because the political class, led by the Presidency, still behaves as if it is from Mars. That is part of the hubris of power. The lack of adequate safety nets for the most vulnerable in the society is a minus for a President who thinks he knows Nigeria. The opposition can turn the tide and make the next few weeks preceding the election uncomfortable for the incumbent if it can focus on affordability issues and the rising cost of living. But it has to show that it has a better alternative beyond rhetoric. It is not by introducing dysfunctional, badly thought out subsidies which could take us back in time. Nigerians don’t want to suffer the pains of the last three years in vain. We need a solid economic blueprint which should take Nigeria to the next level among the comity of nations. The opposition needs to succeed where the incumbent has failed which is to connect with the people in meaningful ways. But first, it has to come together to speak with one voice. Then, it has to articulate its economic direction in more meaningful ways. The post January 2027: Tinubu’s achilles heel, by Muyiwa Adetiba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Supreme Court Justices placed on US visa ban – Retiring jurist
items.description: •Judgement that gave Uzodimma governorship victory fingered By Ikechukwu Nnochiri A retiring Justice of the Supreme Court, Justice Uwani Abba-Aji, disclosed on Friday that some justices of the court had been placed on a visa ban by the United States of America. Read Also : Uzodinma sworn-in as sixth governor of Imo Justice Abba-Aji, speaking during a valedictory session held to mark her retirement from the bench, said the travel ban followed a judgment of the apex court that she described as widely misinterpreted. She said: “My time on the Supreme Court bench was filled with challenges, some of which have served as additional opportunities to stand firm on the side of justice, regardless of the consequences. “One of such challenging judgments was widely misinterpreted and led to a travel ban to the United States of America being imposed on all members of the panel, a ban which still holds today.” Even though Justice Abba-Aji did not mention the specific case that led to the imposition of a US visa ban on Supreme Court Justices, Vanguard understands that it was connected to the legal tussle that followed the 2019 governorship election in Imo State. A seven-member panel of the Supreme Court, which included the current Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, and Justice Abba-Aji, had on January 14, 2020, nullified the election of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate, Emeka Ihedioha, and ordered the swearing-in of the candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Senator Hope Uzodimma, who had initially finished fourth in the governorship election. In the lead judgment delivered by the CJN, the apex court ordered the immediate withdrawal of the Certificate of Return that had already been issued to Ihedioha by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). It ordered that a fresh Certificate of Return be issued to Uzodimma as the validly elected governor of Imo State. To arrive at the decision, the apex court panel vacated the concurrent verdicts of both the Court of Appeal and the Imo State Governorship Election Petitions Tribunal, which had earlier affirmed the PDP candidate as winner of the gubernatorial contest. Votes counted in courtroom The panel went ahead to add election results from 388 polling units, amounting to 213,295 votes, which were tendered before the tribunal by a police officer who testified as PW-54, but which INEC disowned. After all the votes were computed inside the courtroom, Uzodimma was declared the candidate who secured the majority of lawful votes cast at the election, a judgment that elicited wide reactions and protests. Other members of the panel, which was led by the then CJN, Justice Tanko Muhammad, were Justices Sylvester Ngwuta, Kayode Ariwola and Amiru Sanusi. Although Ihedioha subsequently approached the apex court again for a review of the judgment, which he insisted occasioned a miscarriage of justice, his application was refused. Only one member of the panel, Justice Centus Nweze, gave a dissenting verdict that ordered Ihedioha’s reinstatement as governor, declaring the judgment that removed him from office a nullity. Justice Nweze then warned the Supreme Court panel about the consequences of the judgment, which he said was delivered in bad faith. “This decision of the Supreme Court will continue to haunt our electoral jurisprudence for a long time to come,” he warned. Meanwhile, at the valedictory session on Friday, Justice Abba-Aji who is exiting the apex court having reached the 70-year mandatory retirement age, said the US visa ban was part of the price she paid for her service on the bench. “Such inconveniences were a small price to pay to preserve the chastity of justice,” she added. In her address, the CJN, Justice Kekere-Ekun, extolled the virtues of the retiring jurist, who she said had served in various administrative capacities as a Clerical Assistant, Assistant Registrar, Acting Registrar and Higher Registrar since 1973, when she joined the judicial service in Borno State. She noted that Justice Abba-Aji had served at various Divisions of the Court in Benin, Abuja, Ekiti, Owerri and Kaduna since September 22, 2004, when she was elevated to the Court of Appeal, before she was promoted to the Supreme Court on January 8, 2019. “For many of us, particularly the women who have entered the Nigerian Judiciary in more recent years, Hon. Justice Abba-Aji’s career is part of the story of how the place of women in our Judiciary has evolved. “Long before the presence of women on the Bench became as familiar as it is today, she was already serving, quietly establishing a record of competence and service. “Hon. Justice Abba-Aji’s journey into the legal profession began at a time when the professional landscape was very different from what we know today. “Her leadership roles in the Federation of Muslim Women Associations of Nigeria and, particularly, her service as President of the National Association of Women Judges Nigeria (NAWJN), demonstrate that her interest in the progress of women was not merely incidental to her career. “She contributed to creating a space in which other women could find their voices and assume positions of leadership,” the CJN added. Vanguard News The post Supreme Court Justices placed on US visa ban – Retiring jurist appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Man allegedly spends 3 days in cemetery coffin in suspected money ritual at Foase
items.description: A bizarre discovery at a cemetery in Foase in the Atwima Kwanwoma District of the Ashanti Region has left residents unsettled after a hunter reportedly found a 28-year-old drug store operator inside a coffin. The man, identified only as Foster, was discovered on Thursday, November 5, 2026, in a coffin placed in an open area of the community’s cemetery. Residents suspect that he may have been engaged in a money ritual, although the circumstances surrounding his presence at the cemetery remain unclear. According to information gathered, the hunter was passing through the cemetery when he noticed the coffin and became suspicious because it had been left exposed. His dogs reportedly approached the coffin, prompting him to draw his gun and threaten to shoot whoever might be inside. A resident who recounted the incident said the threat forced the occupant to emerge. “After seeing the coffin, his dogs ran to the coffin, so the hunter pointed his gun at the coffin and threatened to shoot whoever is in it, only for the man to come out of it,” the resident said. A herbalist who was also in the vicinity, reportedly on his way to gather herbs, joined the hunter in bringing the man into the community. Their arrival attracted a crowd of residents, many of whom gathered to establish what had happened. Some called for police intervention. The discovery has fuelled speculation among residents, with claims that Foster had allegedly spent three days inside the coffin as part of a suspected money-making ritual. The man was subsequently handed over to the police to assist with investigations into the incident.

items.title: Nepra raises industrial tariff to Rs25.30 per unit, despite dissent
items.description: • Two members oppose revision, saying actual marginal cost stands at Rs31.83/unit • Power regulator warns of package suspension and legal action over missed deadlines • Consumers to pay an additional Rs2.37/unit in Nov bills to recover Rs25bn under fuel cost adjustment ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) on Friday announced a controversial revision of a special electricity tariff introduced as an incentive to revive industrial activity, while approving an additional burden of Rs2.37 per unit on electricity consumers for November. The decision, opposed by the industrial sector, is likely to have a negative impact on all electricity consumers, including those served by K-Electric and other distribution companies (Discos). All four members of the regulator unanimously held the Power Division and its subordinate entities responsible for failing to fulfil their legal obligations within the prescribed timelines, pushing Nepra into an unprecedented deadlock and potentially increasing costs for electricity consumers across the country. At the centre of the controversy was an incremental support package (ISP) of Rs22.98 per unit introduced for industrial consumers in December last year. Industrialists have been protesting against the package since May, seeking its suspension on the grounds that it had failed to benefit them and was instead increasing their electricity bills. The package was due for a review after the completion of its first six months in June, based on the lessons learnt during its implementation. Following a belated request from the Power Division, despite repeated reminders from the regulator, Nepra on Friday revised the ISP rate to Rs25.30 per unit. The decision was strongly opposed by its two most relevant members, those responsible for tariff and development matters. Interestingly, Nepra Chairman Waseem Mukhtar fully endorsed the written arguments and positions taken by the dissenting members but subsequently exercised his special casting vote to approve the revised rate of Rs25.30 per unit instead of retaining the existing rate of Rs22.98. The authority was divided 2-2 on the matter. Member Tariff Amina Ahmed and Member Development Maqsood Anwar, in a joint dissenting note, maintained that even the proposed revised rate of Rs25.30 per unit was a “random number” unsupported by evidence. They said Nepra’s own institutional calculations put the marginal cost at Rs31.83 per unit rather than Rs25.30. “The revised incremental rate of Rs25.30 per unit proposed by the Ministry of Energy (MoE), and allowed by the honourable Chairman and Member (Law), is based on the generation mix apparently assumed at the design stage of the package, with updated fuel prices,” the two members observed. They called for the immediate suspension of the ISP until authentic data became available. The dissenting members argued that compliance with the federal cabinet’s decision and Nepra’s own directives required a reassessment of the existing rate of Rs22.98 per unit to determine whether it should be retained, revised or suspended. However, this exercise had not been carried out, resulting in the continuation of the package at a rate below the actual cost of supplying incremental electricity. “The resulting misalignment has had implications for consumers in two ways. First, to the extent incremental consumption increased the system’s average fuel cost, the resulting impact was recovered from all consumers through the FCA mechanism. Second, because incremental units are excluded from quarterly tariff adjustments, the exclusion of such units increases the quarterly adjustment borne by consumers not availing the package,” they said. The two members, therefore, recommended the temporary suspension of the tariff package rather than choosing the proposed rate of Rs25.30 or above per unit. They questioned how a package based on the principle of cost-reflectivity could continue without a validated cost-reflective rate. They argued that since the alternative rate had no credible link with the actual marginal cost, continuation of the package was no longer justified. They said other consumers should not be made to bear the cost of a review that the MoE was required to submit five months ago but had yet to provide. In his casting vote, Nepra Chairman Waseem Mukhtar observed that the dissenting members’ conclusions “need serious consideration”. However, he said suspending the package at this stage would not be appropriate and that the Ministry of Energy should be given another opportunity to provide the information repeatedly sought by the regulator, including in its latest determination. All four members agreed that the Power Division was required to submit revised calculations six months ago but had failed to do so despite repeated reminders from Nepra. They also regretted that the ministry had not responded adequately to the questions and queries raised by the regulator. “The marginal price, in proper form, was not provided to the regulator by either the Independent System and Market Operator (ISMO) or the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), which were duty-bound to do so. Since the ISP is a flagship project of the ministry, it should give due consideration to the observations of Nepra and the lack of inter-agency coordination among the entities working under the ministry,” the members observed. The determination also sets deadlines for the relevant entities to provide the required information. The four members warned that failure to meet these deadlines could lead to an adverse outcome in the review of the programme, including its suspension or termination. “Furthermore, any entity that fails to provide the required information within the stipulated timeline shall lead to initiation of legal proceedings under the applicable legal framework,” they stated. Explaining his decision, Nepra chairman said: “I hereby exercise, in due and faithful discharge of the functions of the Authority, my second and casting vote envisaged and entrusted to me under the Nepra Act in favour of the First Opinion, thereby breaking the deadlock in relation to the aforesaid issues. Accordingly, the First Opinion constitutes the Order of the Authority.” Meanwhile, Nepra allowed power distribution companies to charge an additional Rs2.37 per unit from all consumers in their November bills under the monthly fuel cost adjustment (FCA) mechanism to recover an additional Rs25 billion. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

items.title: Ouagadougou : La BMCRF ferme des maquis et scelle des boutiques pour pratiques commerciales abusives
items.description: La Brigade mobile de contrôle économique et de répression des fraudes (BMCRF) intensifie ses contrôles dans la capitale burkinabè. À l'issue d'opérations inopinées menées dans plusieurs quartiers de Ouagadougou, des maquis ont été fermés, des boutiques scellées et des produits périmés ou prohibés saisis. Les commerçants épinglés ont également été réquisitionnés pour effectuer des travaux d'intérêt général. Les commerçants en infraction sont désormais prévenus. À Ouagadougou, la Brigade mobile de contrôle économique et de répression des fraudes (BMCRF) multiplie les descentes sur le terrain pour mettre un terme aux pratiques commerciales abusives et veiller au respect de la réglementation. Ces opérations inopinées ont concerné plusieurs secteurs de la capitale, notamment Saaba, Wemtenga, la Patte d'Oie et Nagrin. Les équipes de contrôle ont particulièrement ciblé les dépôts-caves, les débits de boissons, les maquis et les boutiques. Deux préoccupations étaient au centre de cette offensive : le respect des prix conseillés des boissons et la conformité des produits proposés aux consommateurs. Des établissements fermés et des produits saisis Sur le terrain, les contrôleurs ont relevé plusieurs irrégularités. Les sanctions n'ont pas tardé : certains maquis ont été fermés, tandis que des boutiques ont été scellées. Les équipes de la BMCRF ont également procédé à la saisie de produits périmés ou prohibés, retirés des circuits de distribution afin d'éviter qu'ils ne se retrouvent entre les mains des consommateurs. Autre mesure prise contre les commerçants épinglés : leur réquisition pour effectuer des travaux d'intérêt général. Une démarche qui accompagne les mesures de répression engagées contre les pratiques contraires à la réglementation commerciale. La BMCRF appelle les consommateurs à dénoncer les abus À travers ces interventions, la BMCRF entend renforcer la discipline commerciale et préserver les droits des consommateurs face aux pratiques déloyales. L'institution invite également les populations à jouer leur rôle en signalant les irrégularités constatées dans les commerces. Pour dénoncer un abus ou une pratique commerciale suspecte, les citoyens peuvent appeler gratuitement les numéros suivants : – 80 00 11 84 – 80 00 11 85 – 80 00 11 86 Par cette intensification des contrôles, la BMCRF rappelle que la protection des consommateurs passe aussi par la vigilance collective. À Ouagadougou, les commerçants sont ainsi appelés à se conformer aux règles en vigueur, sous peine de sanctions. items.title: Burkina Faso : La vente et l’utilisation du produit « DengueMed » interdites sur toute l’étendue du territoire
items.description: Présenté comme un traitement contre la dengue, le produit « DengueMed » est désormais interdit de vente et d’utilisation au Burkina Faso. La Faso Food and Drug Administration (Faso FDA) alerte sur l’absence d’autorisation de mise sur le marché et l’absence d’évaluation de sa qualité, de son efficacité et de son innocuité. La Faso Food and Drug Administration (Faso FDA) tire la sonnette d’alarme sur la circulation d’un produit présenté comme un remède contre la dengue. Dans un communiqué, l’institution annonce l’interdiction de la vente, de la dispensation, de la prescription, de la détention en vue de la vente et de l’utilisation de « DengueMed » sur toute l’étendue du territoire burkinabè. À l’origine de cette décision, les vérifications effectuées par l’autorité sanitaire ont révélé que le produit ne dispose d’aucune autorisation de mise sur le marché au Burkina Faso. Il ne figure pas non plus dans la nomenclature nationale des spécialités pharmaceutiques et des médicaments génériques autorisés, édition 2026. Plus préoccupant encore, sa qualité, son efficacité et son innocuité n’ont fait l’objet d’aucune évaluation par une autorité compétente. Autrement dit, les garanties nécessaires pour assurer la sécurité des personnes qui pourraient l'utiliser ne sont pas établies. La mesure, prise conformément à la loi n° 23/94/ADP du 19 mai 1994 portant Code de la santé publique, concerne toutes les présentations du produit, quels que soient le lot et le fournisseur. Les pharmacies et formations sanitaires appelées à retirer le produit La décision concerne directement les pharmaciens, les grossistes, les responsables de dépôts pharmaceutiques ainsi que les formations sanitaires publiques et privées. Ces structures sont invitées à retirer immédiatement « DengueMed » de leurs rayons et de leurs stocks, à le mettre en quarantaine et à déclarer les quantités détenues ainsi que l'identité de leurs fournisseurs à la Faso FDA ou à la direction régionale de la santé compétente. Les professionnels de santé doivent également s'abstenir de prescrire, de dispenser ou de recommander ce produit. Les stocks concernés seront récupérés par les équipes d'inspection. La Faso FDA annonce par ailleurs des contrôles dans les officines, les dépôts pharmaceutiques et les formations sanitaires. Les contrevenants s'exposent aux sanctions administratives et pénales prévues par la réglementation en vigueur. La population invitée à la vigilance Au-delà des professionnels de santé, l'autorité sanitaire adresse un message de prudence à l'ensemble de la population : ne pas acheter et ne pas utiliser « DengueMed ». En cas de fièvre, de maux de tête ou de douleurs musculaires et articulaires, il est recommandé de se rendre dans un centre de santé pour bénéficier d'une prise en charge adaptée. La Faso FDA rappelle également qu'en cas de suspicion de dengue, l'aspirine et les anti-inflammatoires comme l'ibuprofène sont à éviter en raison du risque accru de saignement. Certains symptômes doivent particulièrement alerter et conduire à une consultation en urgence. Il s'agit notamment des douleurs abdominales intenses, des vomissements répétés, des saignements du nez ou des gencives, d'une fatigue importante ou d'un état d'agitation. Des numéros pour signaler le produit Pour faciliter le signalement de la présence de « DengueMed » et obtenir des informations complémentaires, la Faso FDA met plusieurs canaux de communication à la disposition des populations et des professionnels de santé : Numéro vert CORUS : 3535 WhatsApp : 52 25 30 30 Facebook : Faso FDA et Laafiako Plateforme numérique : www.laafiako.minsante.bf Courriel : vigilances@fasofda.bf À travers cette interdiction, signée par son directeur général, le Dr Arsène Ouédraogo, la Faso FDA entend prévenir les risques liés à l'utilisation de produits de santé non autorisés et renforcer la protection des populations face à la circulation de traitements dont la sécurité n'est pas établie. items.title: Burkina : Un enfant pourra désormais porté le nom de sa mère, de son clan, de sa ligné
items.description: Un enfant pourra désormais porter le nom de son clan, de sa lignée, de sa mère ou encore le prénom de son père, selon les pratiques coutumières admises. Le Conseil des ministres du 5 novembre 2026 a adopté un décret qui précise les modalités d’attribution du nom de famille conformément aux us et coutumes. Le choix du nom de famille des enfants au Burkina Faso fait l’objet de nouvelles précisions réglementaires. Réuni en Conseil des ministres le jeudi 5 novembre 2026, le gouvernement a adopté un décret fixant les modalités de dévolution du nom de l’enfant conformément aux us et coutumes. Concrètement, le nouveau décret reconnaît plusieurs possibilités dans le choix du nom de famille de l’enfant. Selon le compte rendu du Conseil des ministres, celui-ci pourra porter le nom du clan ou de la lignée auxquels il appartient. Il pourra également recevoir le nom de sa mère, le prénom ou l’un des prénoms de son père, ainsi que toute déclinaison admise du nom de l’un de ses parents. Présentée au titre du ministère de la Justice, cette décision vise à assurer l’application de la loi n°012-2025/ALT du 1er septembre 2025 portant Code des personnes et de la famille au Burkina Faso. Cette disposition ouvre ainsi la possibilité de prendre en compte différentes pratiques traditionnelles dans l'attribution du nom de famille, au-delà des seules formes habituellement utilisées dans les familles. À travers ce texte, les autorités entendent encadrer juridiquement la transmission du nom de l’enfant en tenant compte des réalités socioculturelles burkinabè. L’adoption de ce décret constitue donc une étape dans la mise en œuvre du nouveau Code des personnes et de la famille. Elle apporte des précisions sur les possibilités offertes aux familles pour choisir le nom de leurs enfants dans le respect des us et coutumes reconnus. L’article Burkina : Un enfant pourra désormais porté le nom de sa mère, de son clan, de sa ligné est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Burkina Faso : Une nouvelle société d’économie mixte créée pour renforcer l’approvisionnement en hydrocarbures
items.description: Baptisée TADJI DU FASO (TAFA Energies), cette nouvelle structure aura pour mission de contribuer à la disponibilité des produits pétroliers sur le marché national. La SONABHY détiendra 60 % de son capital, à hauteur de 600 millions de FCFA. Le Burkina Faso renforce son dispositif d’approvisionnement en produits pétroliers. Réuni le jeudi 5 novembre 2026, le Conseil des ministres a adopté un décret portant création de la société d’économie mixte TADJI DU FASO, dénommée TAFA Energies. Cette nouvelle structure a pour objectif de contribuer à assurer la disponibilité des hydrocarbures sur l’ensemble du territoire national, aussi bien en quantité qu’en qualité. Cette participation représente un investissement de 600 millions de FCFA. À travers la création de TAFA Energies, les autorités entendent renforcer les capacités nationales dans le secteur des hydrocarbures et contribuer à une meilleure disponibilité des produits pétroliers pour les consommateurs. Cette initiative intervient dans un contexte où la sécurisation de l’approvisionnement en carburant demeure un enjeu important pour le fonctionnement de l’économie nationale, les activités de transport et les besoins des populations. Les modalités opérationnelles de cette nouvelle société devront permettre de préciser sa contribution au dispositif national de distribution et d’approvisionnement en hydrocarbures. items.title: You entrust officials with $1m but pay them $400 – former Head of Civil Service slams salary structure
items.description: Former Head of the Civil Service, Dr Alex Glover-Quartey, has called for better remuneration for senior public servants, arguing that government cannot expect officials entrusted with millions of dollars in public funds to maintain high standards of integrity while paying them what he describes as inadequate salaries. He said the remuneration of Chief Directors and other senior officials should reflect the scale of their responsibilities, warning that poor pay could create conditions that make corruption and abuse of office more difficult to contain. Dr Glover-Quartey made the remarks in an interview with Kafui Dey, during which he recounted efforts he made while heading the Civil Service to secure improved salaries for officials. He said one of his first engagements in the position was a meeting with representatives of the World Bank and a group from the United Kingdom, whom he sought to persuade to support a monthly salary of about US$2,500 for Chief Directors. He recalled that the proposal initially surprised the representatives, but he questioned the logic of entrusting a senior official with the management of more than US$1 million while paying that person about US$400 a month. “I was trying to convince them to pay salaries that were ahead of, I said, roughly $2,500 a month to chief directors. And they looked shocked,” he said. “And I said, look, you are giving the chief director of a ministry over a million dollars to manage, and you are paying him $400 a month. Is it wisdom? Well, they saw it.” Pay must reflect responsibility Dr Glover-Quartey said Ghana could not continue to offer what he described as paltry salaries to civil servants and still expect them to manage substantial public resources without being exposed to the temptation of misappropriation. He argued that government must first address the remuneration gap if it expects greater accountability and responsible stewardship from public officials. “You cannot continue to pay the pittance that we pay to our civil servants and expect them to manage such huge amounts and not touch them,” he said. He advocated a compensation system that gave senior public servants sufficient financial security, while expecting them to reciprocate through professionalism, discipline and responsible management of public resources. His position places the question of public-sector remuneration at the centre of the broader debate about corruption, institutional performance and accountability in Ghana’s public administration. Rethink allowances and benefits The former Civil Service head also questioned the practice of providing senior officials with extensive utility benefits and other perks when their salaries were not considered adequate. He suggested that government could review arrangements under which public servants receive support for electricity, water and telephone bills, arguing that some of the benefits could be abused. “Stop paying the electricity bills, water bills, telephone bills. In some cases, when you pay, you have free telephone calls and so on; people abuse them,” he said. Ghana’s public service remuneration is administered under the Single Spine Salary Structure, which is intended to promote equity and transparency through a harmonised system of pay and allowances. The Fair Wages and Salaries Commission is responsible for determining and managing salaries for public servants whose pay is drawn from the Consolidated Fund. The policy also provides for standardised allowances, market premiums for scarce skills and performance management. Dr Glover-Quartey, who served as Head of the Civil Service from 2003 to 2006, has previously called for better treatment and improved working conditions for public servants, arguing that the quality of public service delivery depends partly on how the people responsible for implementing government policies are supported. His latest comments renew the debate over whether Ghana’s public-sector pay arrangements adequately reflect the responsibilities of senior officials and what reforms are needed to strengthen integrity and efficiency in public administration.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Le gouvernement dissout le SP/CNLS-IST
items.description: Le Secrétariat permanent du Conseil national de lutte contre le SIDA et les infections sexuellement transmissibles (SP/CNLS-IST) sera dissous. Ses missions et attributions seront désormais assurées par le ministère de la Santé, dans le cadre d’une réorganisation des structures de l’État. Une nouvelle réorganisation se dessine dans le dispositif institutionnel de lutte contre le VIH/SIDA au Burkina Faso. Réuni le jeudi 5 novembre 2026, le Conseil des ministres a adopté un rapport relatif à un projet de décret portant dissolution du Secrétariat permanent du Conseil national de lutte contre le SIDA et les infections sexuellement transmissibles (SP/CNLS-IST). Selon le compte rendu du Conseil des ministres, cette décision s’inscrit dans la volonté du gouvernement de rationaliser la gestion de certaines structures de l’État. Concrètement, la dissolution du SP/CNLS-IST entraîne le transfert de ses missions et de ses attributions au ministère de la Santé. Ce département ministériel sera ainsi chargé d’assurer la continuité des responsabilités jusque-là exercées par le Secrétariat permanent. À travers cette mesure, les autorités entendent réorganiser le fonctionnement de l’administration publique et rationaliser les structures institutionnelles intervenant dans les politiques nationales de santé.
