items.title: Face aux frappes russes incessantes, la capitale ukrainienne peut-elle tenir ?
items.description: La situation dans les grandes villes ukrainiennes s’est considérablement détériorée ces dernières semaines, notamment à Kiev, alors que l’armée russe accélère sa campagne de frappes sur les réseaux de production et de distribution d’électricité. Les centrales de production, lignes à haute tension et sous-stations sont prises pour cible de manière systématique : 238 frappes ayant touché des infrastructures énergétiques ont été recensées en octobre, selon ACLED. Il s’agit d’un record depuis le début de l’invasion à grande échelle, en février 2022. Les centrales thermiques de Kiev ne produisent plus d’électricité, et la capitale dépend en majorité de trois centrales nucléaires situées à environ 300 kilomètres. Les longues distances parcourues par les lignes à haute tension pour transporter le courant depuis l’ouest et le sud du pays vers la capitale rendent la ville très vulnérable aux attaques, notamment car la portée des drones russes dépasse aujourd’hui les 1 000 kilomètres. Les autorités de Kiev ont développé un réseau de petites centrales à gaz qui permettent d’assurer le fonctionnement de services essentiels – hôpitaux, une partie des stations de pompage d’eau, etc. –, mais celles-ci ne couvrent qu’une fraction des besoins de la ville. Volodymyr Zelensky a décrit vendredi 6 novembre la situation énergétique à Kiev comme « la pire » du pays, évoquant des défis « très sérieux » Publication sur Telegram de Volodymyr Zelensky , 6 novembre 2026.'> 9 . En plus des coupures d’électricité, des frappes russes ont privé mardi 3 novembre l’ensemble de la capitale d’eau pendant plus de 24 heures, selon les autorités municipales Russian strikes cause Kyiv’s worst water outage of full-scale war », The Kyiv Independent , 4 novembre 2026.'> 10 . La situation pourrait davantage se dégrader étant donné l’asymétrie entre les capacités offensives russes et défensives ukrainiennes. La Russie serait en mesure de tirer entre 130 et 190 projectiles balistiques par mois cet hiver. Ces vecteurs sont trop rapides pour être interceptés par des drones ou d’autres moyens low cost , et nécessitent des intercepteurs An Important Message : The Coming Winter in Ukraine », Missile Matters – with Fabian Hoffmann , 1er novembre 2026.'> 11 . Or, l’Ukraine ne reçoit en moyenne que 12 missiles intercepteurs Patriot livrés par les États-Unis chaque mois, soit moins de 5 % du nombre nécessaire. Les intercepteurs européens, comme les missiles Aster du système SAMP/T, ne compensent qu’à la marge. En octobre, l’Ukraine n’a abattu que 11 des 150 missiles balistiques tirés par la Russie – soit environ 7 %. L’hiver 2026-2027 sera vraisemblablement le plus difficile pour les Ukrainiens depuis le début de la guerre à grande échelle. La stratégie russe vise à rendre la capitale du pays inhabitable, en ciblant les infrastructures qui assurent le chauffage, l’éclairage ou l’approvisionnement en eau, afin de faire pression sur la population et d’user son moral. La Banque nationale d’Ukraine estime que l’intensification des bombardements russes sur les infrastructures du pays amputera la croissance ukrainienne de près de 2 points en 2026 Національний банк України підвищив облікову ставку до 16,5 % , Banque nationale d'Ukraine, 29 octobre 2026.'> 12 . Le PIB réel devrait se contracter de 0,4 % cette année, pour la première fois depuis 2022. Il avait enregistré une hausse de 1,8 % en 2025, 3,2 % en 2024 et 5,5 % en 2023. L’article Face aux frappes russes incessantes, la capitale ukrainienne peut-elle tenir ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Breaking Down Tech’s Brutal Election
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Data centers, megadonors, and corruption had a bad Election Night. Prediction markets did just fine, but were a bit overhyped. So will the midterm results change how tech leaders move forward? What will a Democratic Congress mean for their businesses? In this episode, Charlie Warzel gets into what this election changes for the tech world, how voters saw through AI ads and billionaire donors, and whether we’re moving into a post–Elon Musk political era. The following is a transcript of the episode: Mike Isaac: I feel like there’s such intense pushback on the data centers specifically. And this is not a new idea, but like it really is this physical manifestation of economic insecurity; that fighting against AI in the ether is much harder to do. But if you’re like, No, this is a giant cube that I hate, that is in my backyard, that represents my doom ultimately —yeah, that’s kind of a layup in a lot of ways, you know? Charlie Warzel: It’s just a national pain sponge, right? Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . You may have noticed there was an election on Tuesday night. Democrats won big, Elon Musk lost big. Millions of dollars flooded into prediction markets. People across the country cast ballots on data-center initiatives, and they told surveyors and exit polls how they felt about megadonors, corruption, and artificial intelligence. One of the big stories of the last few years is the way that many tech leaders and investors have aligned themselves with Donald Trump in his second term. It’s an issue that’s polarized Silicon Valley, and in very important ways, changed the trajectory of technologies like AI and crypto. And on Tuesday night, we learned a lot about how Americans feel about that realignment and about the influence that some of Silicon Valley’s richest people have in our politics. We also got a chance to see how AI, prediction markets, and tech money shaped or didn’t shape electoral outcomes. And so today on Galaxy Brain , we are breaking down what the midterms meant for the tech world. Did prediction markets win the night? Was this the AI election? What happens next for Elon Musk, for the companies who bent the knee to Trump, for the AI labs? We’re taping this on Wednesday right after the midterms, and we’re going to be splitting this conversation up into two conversations. First, I’ll be talking with Mike Isaac, who has covered Silicon Valley for The New York Times for over a decade, and in December he’ll be writing about all of it for us here at The Atlantic . Then I’m going to talk about prediction markets with Will Gottsegen. He’s my colleague who writes the Over/Under newsletter for The Atlantic , which covers risk and prediction markets. Mike Isaac joins me to talk about it now. [ Music ] Warzel: Mike Isaac, my future colleague, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Isaac: Thank you for having me. Warzel: What was, in your mind, the biggest story of the night in tech? Isaac: I mean, personally the biggest story was it feeling like 2014 Twitter vibes again to me. My favorite—this was just very funny culturally—was like, I saw this term come up: I’m not doomscrolling; I’m hopescrolling , a lot of people have been saying. Which is like, you know, obviously a huge wipeout for Republicans across the board, I think. But as far as Techland goes, you know, there was a very clear referendum across I wanna say 40-something ballots—that data centers and this sort of inexorable trudge of AI into everyone’s towns is getting held up. You know, is getting pushed back by a lot of voters. And I think folks in the Valley, at least the ones that I’ve been talking to so far, have been kinda trying to reckon with that and say, Okay, how do we change our positions? I think what they’ll do—I think what the companies will do—is be like, It’s a messaging issue. We’re not telling the right story. All they’ve heard from us has been doom and gloom. You know, certain companies are like, Dario Amodei over at Anthropic is really screwing us, because all he does is talk about how this is gonna destroy the world and take our jobs, but we need to do it. And so my guess is that they’ll try to massage the messaging and say: Here’s, you know, drug discovery. Here’s ways that AI can improve the world. You need to learn how to have it augment your job rather than replace you entirely. But I think that, you know, it’s always gonna come back to that. Because fundamentally there are people who just think it’s not good for the world—developing this technology, certain versions of this technology, is not good for the world. And I think that doesn’t square with a lot of the worldviews among some camps in Silicon Valley who do think it’s just an unmitigated good, no matter how many rocky patches we go through. Like, how do you wrestle with that on a fundamental level, on a human level, when people are repudiating everything you’re trying to do, you know? Warzel: I’m curious; there was some debate going into this, like, you know, This is gonna be the AI election. And then there was I believe our mutual friend Casey Newton argued in his newsletter Platformer last week that this would not be the AI election. And some of that was like, voter anxieties were—economic concerns were much more a factor than something like AI and data centers. Turns out maybe that wasn’t necessarily true. But also I think what Casey was referring to is the idea that people were worried about a lot of AI deepfakes or, you know, potential misinformation. Or chatbots leading people to different canonical answers about who to vote for, or whatnot. And I’m just curious: In your mind, was this the “AI election”? How should we be framing that? Isaac: That’s a really good point. So I do actually believe that people can care about what role AI has in society and not make it their platform issue, right? Like, I do think at the end of the day, a lot of voters were like, I care that gas is now three times what it was before and that I can’t afford groceries, and I’m not sure why we’re at war abroad with a country that I don’t think about in my daily life. Like I absolutely think those are pretty high on the priority list for a lot of voters who turned out. And so in that regard, I don’t think it’s necessarily the AI election, I think. And it goes back to like: Okay, at the end of the day, I can’t afford to feed my family. I have this company or whatever sort of changing things in my community in a way that I don’t like, or I’m worried about. And I have folks maybe saying, like, “China’s gonna come get me,” or whatever. We’re gonna be, like, unprepared for the future—but I’m not as much worried about the future as I am just getting my day-to-day life sorted out, and trying to figure out how to put food on the table. And so in that sense, I think it’s also not the AI election. Or at least I’m starting to give voters more credit as far as, you know, seeing through some of the “online is gonna control your minds” sort of stuff, in a way that I don’t think was as present, as maybe folks had been worried about, just a few years ago. If that makes sense. Warzel: No, I think so. And I think you see it in the ways that propaganda and AI slop and all that kind of stuff has factored into this election. Like, it’s not moving people to believe, most of the time. There’s obviously always exceptions, but it’s not, most of the time, leading people to believe a reality that doesn’t exist. It seems to be a tool to augment the kind of political messaging that we’re always very used to, right? Like, crazy attack ads. I saw an analysis from the AI-detection company CopyLeaks that 47 percent of governor races published an AI-generated campaign ad of some kind in this cycle, right? Isaac: Wow. Bring back human-centered oppo. Warzel: But I think it speaks a little to—it’s like, yeah, this is just a way that we’re gonna illustrate a lot of this stuff, right? We’re gonna make people look bad in this way. And it’s not to say that it doesn’t matter, but that it’s sort of slotting into something that people are used to, and that people really know how to navigate, right? Like, people understand, I think—now this far into elections dominating the American psyche. You see a lot of attack ads, and you’re either sort of like, God , or you’re like, That’s interesting . I think you’re so right to just be giving voters and normal people a lot more credit for navigating this information environment in this cycle. Isaac: I’m wondering, especially with some of the young-voter turnout, if we’re hitting this new generation of folks that can see through that much easier. And I’m also fearing the moment where I start getting duped by stuff and I’ve hit the cliff of my BS detective. Warzel: It’s, well, the AI-agent stuff, and the spoofing. Like, I’m not so worried about it with politics. I am worried about it, you know, with my bank account. Speaking of money, I wanna talk about the money that poured into this. One of the obviously major stories of Tuesday night was that Elon Musk donated almost $500 million this election cycle, the single largest non-candidate donor in any election ever. A lot of that money went toward the Texas Senate race, where James Talarico drubbed Ken Paxton. And I am curious: What, in your mind, did Musk think he was buying? Isaac: The more I’ve been thinking about this playing out, Musk has always been. And money in politics obviously is not a new thing. But it’s always been this thing of, like: Here comes the richest man in the world, and he can do what he wants, and he can throw all this money and everything. And I’m just wondering if part of this race was a referendum on it; like, is there political baggage being attached to him at this point? Like, I don’t know how much the average person cares about Elon Musk. But I do think that, you know, getting blitzed with ads for a candidate who was, in Paxton’s case, very unpopular to begin with in Texas, and seen as a risk for Trump to throw weight behind him, instead of [John] Cornyn was like a real interesting moment on, you know: Is money just gonna work here? Can you just use those millions of dollars and push this candidate? I think it’s very clear that didn’t work, obviously. And now Musk is in a real sticky situation on what his businesses are gonna look like in Texas. But do you think that being attached to Musk, does that change in this new environment? Like, it makes me wonder about, kind of how being attached to Trump. And, you know, even now the coverage is shifting from Are we in a post-Trump world, or whatever? Are we moving to a post-Musk era of politics? If that makes sense? Warzel: Well, I think that, unfortunately for Musk, he really represented every single faction that on Tuesday night America said that they were tired of, right? Like, he is an oligarch. He’s one of the—he’s the richest man in the world. He is in the business of AI, but also explicitly building data centers in communities, including historically Black communities. He is totally aligned with the MAGA movement, obviously, and with DOGE and all that stuff. It’s all rolled into one person, right? And so I do think, in some ways, even like it was just tailor-made that it was gonna be a little bit of a referendum on him, or you can see how easily that worked. And obviously, you know Talarico and others made this election in a lot of ways about someone buying it, right? About either Musk or other megadonors buying that election. And so I think that was very interesting. To your other point, I wanna get to that in a second, but the way that I was kind of thinking about what he was also trying to buy, though, is: I think he is always like he is a master storyteller, right? And I think that the way that you see that, you know, with SpaceX, with Tesla, he builds things that are consequential and that matter. But he’s also somebody—like when you look at all of Elon Musk’s companies, the price-to-earnings ratio is different than a lot of regular companies that build things in the real world. Meaning that the market values them a lot more than their revenues suggest the market should value them, because of the stories that Elon Musk tells. And I kind of think that spending that money, the ways that he has in these last two elections—being the largest donor, being just very clear about that—I think in a way, it rhymes a little bit, right? It tells a story, win or lose, about Elon Musk as this person who can drop half a billion dollars and have that loss made up in, you know, 45 seconds of SpaceX trading on the stock exchange. And I think that there is just something of, like—it adds to the myth of Elon Musk in this way. It makes him central. Like, there’s no reason we should be talking about him in this election. He’s the CEO of a bunch of companies. And yet. He is one of the headlining stories because of all of that. Isaac: He does kinda have main-character energy all the time, right? It seems like he likes that. He always likes redirecting the spotlight toward himself. In some ways, might become a liability in some of this stuff. I don’t know. Warzel: I think that is what is gonna be really interesting here, because Musk, with all this, did ingratiate himself to this movement, right? He’s in a way, maybe not single-handedly, but independently, kept some of these campaigns afloat, kept them from totally crashing to the ground. And it’s an odd thing, because he has further yoked himself to this movement that now feels no longer ascendant. But also at the same time I don’t know that they can just turn their back on him. He does seem to be like a real chance for them. I’m not sure. I mean, do you get the sense that everyone’s gonna drop Musk like a bad habit after all of this? Isaac: You know, it’s really the way—as you’re talking about this, I do think there are parallels to reckoning with the role of Trump in the Republican Party and the role of Musk in the Republican Party, right? And I think there was—because Trump has remade the party in his image for the past decade, and now voters seem to say there are limits to that, I think the GOP has to really reckon with what that means, and what that looks like for campaigning in the future. I really think there’s probably gonna be a similar sort of thinking about what that means with Musk, and attaching yourself to Musk, for a number of candidates. I don’t think that means “drop it like a bad habit.” I think at least not for everyone, you know. But I feel like there’s gonna be at least a little bit of backpedaling in a way that doesn’t completely alienate oneself from Elon’s dollars, which are, as you said, pretty important in a lot of ways. So I just feel like this period is gonna be such a struggle, too, for both the candidates and the CEOs at some of these companies, beyond Musk, trying to figure out: What is our next move? And really, our next talking points? [Music] Warzel: I was interested in your read on a tweet that Sam Altman put out last night, where he wrote: “People should always be in control of the future. OpenAI is against the notion that it would be acceptable for people to be relegated to a role of doing things that ‘AI systems think makes sense to rewarding humans.’ People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence.” It sounds a little, Yep. I understand now we’re gonna be maybe regulated in some way or that there will be some constraints to us. I’m curious of your read on that, and if that felt to you like an acknowledgement that things were maybe gonna have to change a little bit. Isaac: Yeah, I mean, it was funny. That’s like the only big CEO that I’ve seen really say anything even remotely a little bit political, so far. The only other thing was Musk deleting his “go vote for red” tweets, which was kind of funny. But I hope everyone didn’t see it. But I do think it sets up an interesting dynamic. Right now, OpenAI and Altman are staring very hard at Anthropic, on the eve of their IPO in the next couple of weeks. And their strategy has really been to paint themselves as a foil to Dario Amodei and Anthropic being the bad guys here, and sort of trying to cast themselves as the sane ones, where Dario is this doomer who thinks, you know, AI is gonna kill us all. And lead the charge, and only they are the ones that can harness it. Because it is inevitable. It wasn’t that long ago that Sam was talking about these things in a very similar way. But I do think if you’re the CEO of an AI company and you see a pretty strong repudiation of, you know, AI-data-center building across the board, you have to start talking in a way where it’s like, Actually we’re the good AI company, and we want to give you control. And it’s these other guys that are trying to push this stuff down your throat. And also, you know, Dario is kind of hamstrung in what he can say, because they’re in this quiet period before the IPO. So it’s just like, I really admire how ruthless OpenAI is at every turn on their messaging, especially when they’re trying to go after. It reminds me a lot of [Mark] Zuckerberg too. They just—Anthropic is the punching bag of the day, and that’s how I read a lot of their statements these days. Warzel: I’m curious where you think we’re headed here. And so I saw some people posting about, you know, There’s gonna be televised trials of big tech executives, and things like this. And Senator Ed Markey posted on X last night: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all the subpoenas we’ll be printing.” Which is, you know, kind of intense. Isaac: Wow. My God. Yeah. Warzel: Definitely signals a real, almost frothing desire to, you know, make an example out of some of these people. Obviously with Musk and DOGE and all these things, there could be that bringing him to bear; investigating his companies in some way. But I am curious with this. If you think there is—A) what you think could potentially happen. But B) I see this a little bit, and also worry that there could be an overplaying of the hand, like very quickly. So I am curious what you think might happen. And also if you feel any of this, you know, concern about maybe even just like re-radicalizing them again, and just this ping-ponging cycle of techlash, embrace, techlash, embrace . Isaac: Yeah, I mean, I do think accountability often can play well in these moments. Especially when a lot of folks have felt helpless at a president who’s been very, you know, very willing to sort of push through his agenda, and the agenda of like a large vocal faction of his party. Like, I’m not fully convinced that just being a full anti-tech platform is necessarily a winning platform across the board immediately. Just because I do think it’s an issue for many, but it’s not the primary issue. But that doesn’t mean, you know, don’t do anything, or don’t like have investigations that they feel they need to have. I think those are probably gonna go on. But I think there’s gonna be some senators and some representatives who are very fixated on this, who are gonna ask—you know, have investigations into what went down in DOGE. And is there real accountability here? Like, I think that’s a real thing. But I still think, at the end of the day, people are just very upset with the economy and their ability to exist and function in the United States as a family that, you know, can work and afford to feed and clothe themselves. And so—does that mean no reining in of unlimited tech power? Or like, these CEOs just going to Washington and getting a rubber stamp on whatever they’re trying to do? No; I think there’s gonna be real questions around whether that was a good thing or whether that should continue. And that is the prerogative of folks in different places. I guess the other thing I would say is: The reason I feel like there’s such intense pushback on the data centers specifically is—and this is not a new idea—but like it really is this physical manifestation of economic insecurity; that fighting against AI in the ether is much harder to do. But if you’re like, No, this is a giant cube that I hate, that is in my backyard, that represents my doom ultimately —yeah, that’s kind of a layup in a lot of ways, you know? Warzel: Yeah. I’ve thought about it as just—it’s a national pain sponge, right? You could just direct all of your frustrations to it. But also I think, very truly, not only is it the physical manifestation and the cube of doom in your town, but it’s also: You can go to a meeting and yell at somebody about it, and then they will maybe, you know, pull the contract or do whatever, right? Whereas we have seen you can yell a lot at any of the tech executives, and it’s probably not often gonna do a whole heck of a lot. Isaac: That’s right. Yeah. They go to Congress, and they take their drubbing and the viral social-media clips come out of it. With Zuckerberg, you know, looking like he got called into the principal’s office. And then they go home and do whatever they want, basically. And I think that’s far less satisfying to the average person than going to your town hall and saying directly to someone, We don’t want this , and them having to listen to you, basically. Warzel: So I wanna end by doing the absolutely most annoying media thing. Which is: An election just happened, and then we’re gonna talk about the next one that is legitimately two years away. Isaac: God. Warzel: And I’m only curious though, from the idea that, you know, OpenAI is doing some—OpenAI’s top lobbyist, Chris Lehane, is doing some lobbying right now, telling prospective 2028 candidates that artificial intelligence is going to define their bids for the White House. You’re seeing that posturing. Do you think that AI is going to be a much bigger deal? Like, we have in this conversation gone back numerous times, in a way that I think’s super important, that the economy, affordability, these basic issues of being able to live are like the core things. And all these other things bubble up around them, and, you know, impact the way that people vote and they talk about it. But I am curious: We’re on this trajectory with artificial intelligence, where it’s just moving faster and faster, having more and more consequential stakes in our lives. How are you thinking about the role it might play in 2028? Isaac: I mean, look; I think you can tie it to exactly the things we keep returning to. Which is if you believe that this is the trajectory, then these two are on a collision course. It’s going to reshape the—I mean, it already has reshaped our economy in a lot of ways. And the way that you’ve talked about it with the stock market, and basically how the entire stock market and our retirement funds are propped up on the strength of big tech and data-center buildout and a large swathes of employment. So I think that is certainly a key issue, and that’s unavoidable in a lot of ways. The thing that always kinda drives me insane around AI discussions that a lot of folks, a lot of prominent commentators, frame it is just sort of this air of inevitability that I just don’t subscribe to. I think this is—let’s say an election is actually the best way to look at that. Which is like: People have agency, and they have choices to what things are gonna be a part of their lives, and how we are deciding what to build or what not to build, you know? And I think now, as let’s say existential risks or at least safety—if not going as far as to wipe out humanity, but let’s say, like, cybersecurity problems or bioterrorism questions. As this becomes a more mainstream discussion, I think people are gonna actually have opinions on it and what they want—rather than sit back and be told by the influencer of the week that: This is coming; you have to prepare for it no matter what. And I think that’s an empowering message. I think you can talk to people like human beings and say, You should have a seat at the table and decide: Do you want this to be a part of our lives or not? You know? And where I’ll come to common ground with tech executives here is that messaging may be an issue here. Because I do think people should learn about it and understand it, as they decide whether or not they wanna, you know, push back on it. But I think that’s a good thing. To end on, like, a corny note, that’s part of a healthy democracy. And so maybe we’ll get there in the next election. Warzel: It’s also an opportunity, I think, right? Like, I saw Derek Thompson talking about this today—this idea that if you are anti–any regulation whatsoever, and you are investing in a way that is reckless, or that could lead to a bubble that pops and dramatically crashes the stock market and, you know, has all these super-negative effects in the world, and also on the development of the technology? That’s bad if you’re these technology companies. If you build it responsibly, with some meaningful consensus of, you know, the constituents of the world or your country or whatever, and you build it in such a way that if a bubble pops a little bit, there’s not as much economic fallout—and people don’t get hurt and then aren’t totally negatively polarized against you? That’s good for the technology. So to kind of close it out—there’s an opportunity here, I think, for these companies if they want to see it. If they want to do that, as you said, that self-reflection, and that building the consensus around something that all of us are going to have to use and live with and have it affect our lives. So. Isaac: “Self-Aware Tech CEOs 2028?” That’s my headline. Warzel: It’s a big question mark. Mike, this is a delight. Thank you for coming on Galaxy Brain and hashing it out with all of us. Isaac: It’s an honor to be here. I can’t wait to be your colleague very soon. Warzel: First of many. Sweet. [ Break ] Warzel: Will, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Will Gottsegen: Thanks for having me, Charlie. Warzel: I’ve seen a lot of postmortems in the past few hours coming out here saying that prediction markets won the night. Is that framing feeling true to you, or is that overstated? Gottsegen: Yeah; I would say it’s overstated. I don’t love that framing for a few reasons. The first reason is that it’s not clear to me what these markets are bringing to the table that’s not already out there, right, in the ether. I think one of the original ideas behind prediction markets is that they sort of surface the wisdom of the crowd. People in the world go out and they see what’s around them, and they bring that information to the market. And then they make bets on that information. And it informs, you know, the ultimate probability that these platforms put out there. I think we saw that in many of these races, people seem to be sort of making bets on the polls, right—other election forecasts, things they saw on late-night TV broadcasts. It’s hard to know exactly what goes into the predictions that traders are making, but it’s not always clear to me that in every race they’re bringing something new to the table. And so in that way, it’s not clear to me that the night was a huge win for prediction markets. I also think it’s important to remember, you know, these are sort of just sports-betting platforms with prediction markets. Like, they’re sports-betting platforms with politics functions kind of slapped on. These are a small portion of the total volume. I mean, it’s true of both Kalshi and Polymarket. Sports is really, and parlays and crypto—these are sort of where the action is. And last night didn’t change that, really. I mean, we saw a huge sort of marketing campaign around these platforms’ ability to properly forecast elections. We saw billboards go up. We saw massive, like—blockbuster ad campaigns, videos. But it’s not clear to me, yeah, that the calculus has changed that much for the people who are actually using these platforms and making money on them, or not making money on them. Warzel: That’s an interesting thing—about them being sports-betting platforms with politics kind of tacked on. Because I’ve heard it argued that elections should be the best proof of concept for prediction markets, right? ’Cause there’s lots of time for these narratives to develop; lots of data in terms of pretty consistent polling and things happening in the news. There are these big events, and the markets theoretically should be pretty liquid. Meaning that there’s a lot of trading volume in them, a lot of money going into them. Are they the best test, you think, for the efficacy of a prediction market? Or is this really just, as you say, sports betting with a political veneer? Gottsegen: I think it’s just like—what do you want your betting platform to be? What do you want it to do for you? You know what I mean? Like, I think that it’s important narratively for these companies that election forecasts work as they’re expected to. And I think there’s a lot of evidence that they do kind of work as they’re expected to, right? Like, especially when you have a lot of volume. I think in lower-volume situations you can get sort of these whiffs of manipulation, right? Like, it’s not to say they’re rigged. They’re not rigged. But it’s like you can have a smaller bet, a smaller amount of money that moves the market more—just because there’s not a lot of, you know, money sloshing around in the market. But when you’ve got a lot of volume, these things do kinda work as they’re expected to. The problem is that narratively, if you’re these companies, you have to convince the regulators, many of which are against you. You have to convince the American people—many of which are against you or skeptical of you—that you’re doing something for them that is more than just speculation. And so election forecasts are important for that narrative in some ways. You know, they have—these platforms have other ways of trying to make that point, too. But elections are part of that. And like I said, right, the volume situation hasn’t totally changed. People do use these platforms for speculation. They do also use them for other reasons, but the proportion between those two things is just really wildly out of whack. Warzel: What is your sense as to whether this legitimized the prediction markets? Whether it did what they needed—which is give them that veneer of utility as, you know, not just a speculative market? Gottsegen: I do think it’s too soon to tell. But I also think that if it had gone the other way, right, and Republicans had staged a comeback, or if there were really prominent races where people were like, “Wow, the prediction markets really missed.” There were a couple races where, you know, the favorite didn’t win. But if there was no blue wave, say, I think we would’ve seen some major pushback in terms of the credibility and the reputation of these platforms. ’Cause sort of like I was saying, I mean—most Americans are opposed to betting on elections. You know, these markets need to be markets, really. They can’t just be sort of like pure information harvesters. But yeah—it’s not clear to me whether that’s gonna go away based on last night. Warzel: Well, it’s also interesting too, because in some ways you could interpret this election as a bit of a referendum on some of this corruption—on some of this feeling that markets are out of control. That, you know, people are betting on everything. The insider-trading idea and the prediction markets, you know, kind of—I don’t know. It feels interesting to me, in that sense that this could be a good night for them. But also, it does seem like people are starting to get kind of tired of the hollow speculative feeling. When CNN announced its partnership with Kalshi. And anecdotally, it felt like I kept hearing about these prediction markets, you know, integrating themselves, intertwining themselves in with media systems, both traditional and not. I spent some time watching some of these Election Night broadcasts. Didn’t really see a ton of that integration, or as much as I expected. I didn’t see, like, the Kalshi big board on CNN. It was a lot of John King just doing, you know, what he normally does, which is look at the results as they come in. I also didn’t feel like it was a dominant factor. It kind of felt like we put prediction markets on this pedestal, right? We talk about them a lot. And then when the rubber meets the road, when the returns are coming in, it sort of felt like: Okay, now it’s time for, you know, the adults to step up. Like, Decision Desk, AP. Like—the people who call the shots. Did that feel like an accurate description of what you saw? Gottsegen: Totally. I think, like, another thing I’d add to that is that these markets—they’re built to resolve after a certain outcome happens in the world. And with a lot of these elections, that outcome was basically when the networks called it. So there were cases where the markets, you know, would basically home in on a 99 percent probability of a candidate winning. But then there’d be a couple more hours of trading. Like, in other words—the prediction markets sort of called it early. I mean, even on their social media they would call it early. But at the end of the day, the thing that stopped the trading was the networks calling it. So there’s a way in which they’re still relying on the old system. You know, the incumbents aren’t gone in the way that some of these firms might like them to be. There’s been a narrative that prediction markets are better than polls. I mean, they’re not polls, so they’re kind of apples to oranges in that regard. But yeah, I would also say, like—some of this is probably just, like, inertia, right? Like, these are weird tools. These are weird phenomena. I mean, people aren’t ready in some ways to accept them as a part of Election Night. I mean, Kalshi had midterms watch parties. Polymarket had a midterms stream that was going on. But I think for most people, they’re not necessarily tuning into these in the way that maybe finance people are starting to. Warzel: I have a question about the logistics of this, which is if everyone bet on the conventional wisdom, right? Democrats were gonna have a pretty good night. The prediction markets are showing that, because people are betting that way. It’s the way that the polls are looking. And then it worked out, roughly speaking, across the board. Did these companies lose a lot of money? Like, help me understand how this works on a very basic level—if this is good business for them if, you know, they kinda go chalk on the predictions and everything works out exactly the way it’s supposed to be. Gottsegen: Sure. I would say that, you know, the way these platforms make money is trading fees, in large part. And the more trades you get, the more fees they’re raking in. So in some ways, volume is king in this regard. And that’s why a lot of the revenue here comes from sports. Like I said, this didn’t really move the needle. I mean, there was an uptick in volume, clearly. But when it comes to the bottom line for these platforms, sports is where it’s at. And I’m not gonna say it’s de minimis politics, but it’s certainly a very small piece of the pie. So it’s hard to say that, you know, they were either gonna make or lose a lot of money from one night in this case. Warzel: Was there anything that unfolded over the last couple of days, and especially on Election Night, that surprised you? You’ve been covering this, anticipating this moment. Was there anything that stood out or shocked you? Gottsegen: I think what shocked me, if anything shocked me about this, I think it’s sort of a corollary to what you were saying earlier, right? We have known that these platforms have been gunning to be these accurate, unbiased sources of information. They’ve been making these big claims about the fact that they can call races early, the fact that they can aggregate all sorts of new information and bring it to market. And like you said, I think there’s just not a sense that a lot of people are buying into this yet. I mean, certainly finance people are. Certainly people who are on the cutting edge of tech are into this stuff. But there’s such a skepticism. I mean, even anecdotally, from people in my life. I tell them, like, I was watching the Kalshi midterm stuff all night , and they’re like—they just raise an eyebrow. Like you said, I think there might be a reason that this stuff has almost been downplayed on cable news. It’s just, like, not something that people are ready for yet, in certain ways. I mean, in some ways they are, right? There’s “product-market fit.” Like, people love to bet on these platforms. But when it comes to elections, there’s an inherent weirdness there that I think people aren’t ready to grapple with. Warzel: What did Tuesday’s results change, if anything, about how the platforms might be regulated or treated going forward by lawmakers? Gottsegen: It’s a really good question. You know, I think the expectation broadly is that a lot of these sort of roughly ambiguous legal status of whether these things are “gambling.” Whether they are, as they say, prediction markets, whether they’re straight-up markets, right? Whether they’re—whether we’re trading swaps on these platforms or not. I think a lot of that has the potential to be decided in a Supreme Court case. And so until then, you’re gonna see a little bit of what’s been going on already. There’s sort of a patchwork of state regulations that have been pretty loosely applied to these companies. And I think, just sort of like I was saying earlier, the more Dems you have that are sort of opposed to these platforms in theory, maybe you’re gonna get some more hostile regulation. Warzel: I think that we are living in this, as we talked about, this very interesting space where prediction markets got the blue wave—the blue tsunami, whatever you wanna call it—correct. And as a result, they are now much more open to potential regulation or slaps on the wrist. Or, you know, simply just an askance eye from the Congress that they helped predict is gonna come into session. I think that alone is a weirdness and a really interesting wrinkle to this whole phenomenon. Gottsegen: Yeah. It’s sort of—you know, they were rooting for this outcome, because that’s what bettors were forecasting. And if they won, it would sort of help lend credence to this idea that Polymarket and Kalshi are good election forecasters. But right—like you’re saying, there is a potential downside to this on the regulatory side. Warzel: I think that’s a great place to leave it. Will, thank you so much for joining Galaxy Brain . Thank you for your service in tracking all this, and we will continue to follow along with Over/Under. Thank you. That’s it for us here. Thank you to my guests, Will and Mike. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page or on Apple or Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

items.title: Images IA, pourquoi leur utilisation peut tromper le public ?
items.description: Les outils d'intelligence artificielle permettent aujourd'hui de creer presque toutes sortes d'images : paysages, bâtiments, scenes de catastrophes, manifestations ou situations de conflit. De plus en plus realistes, ces productions peuvent facilement etre confondues avec de veritables photographies. Dans le domaine de l'information, cette possibilite souleve une question importante, jusqu'ou peut-on utiliser une image artificielle pour illustrer un fait reel ? Le probleme ne reside pas uniquement dans la creation de ces images, mais surtout dans la maniere dont elles sont presentees et utilisees. Lorsqu'une image generee par IA est associee a un evenement reel sans indication claire, elle peut donner au public une representation erronee des faits. L'utilisation d'une image generee par l'intelligence artificielle pour illustrer un evenement reel comporte plusieurs risques. Elle peut montrer des degâts qui n'existent pas, ou donner une ampleur differente a un evenement. Elle peut egalement associer une personne a une situation qu'elle n'a jamais vecue. Quelles consequences pour le public ? Le premier risque est la confusion. Un internaute qui decouvre une image accompagnant un article ou une publication peut naturellement penser qu'elle montre la situation reelle. Une telle publication peut alors influencer sa comprehension de l'evenement. Dans le cas d'une catastrophe naturelle, elle peut faire croire a des destructions plus importantes ou situees dans un autre quartier. Dans un contexte de crise, une image artificielle peut alimenter des tensions entre communautes. Les consequences peuvent aussi concerner les personnes representees. Enfin, lorsque les medias utilisent des images artificielles sans transparence, ils risquent de fragiliser la confiance du public dans l'information et dans les photos authentiques. Dans quels contextes peut-on utiliser une image generee par IA ? L'intelligence artificielle n'est pas incompatible avec le journalisme. Son utilisation peut etre pertinente lorsque l'image sert a expliquer ou a illustrer un sujet sans pretendre documenter un evenement reel. Une image generee peut representer la desinformation, la cybersecurite, l'intelligence artificielle ou les mecanismes d'une arnaque en ligne. C'est-a-dire les concepts abstraits. Elle peut accompagner des exercices d'education aux medias, des tutoriels ou des scenarios fictifs destines a apprendre au public a reconnaître les fausses informations. Aussi, une illustration artificielle peut aider a visualiser un mecanisme difficile a photographier, a condition de ne pas la presenter comme une observation reelle. En plus, une scene historique ou une situation passee peut etre representee artificiellement si elle est clairement identifiee comme une reconstitution et si elle ne pretend pas etre une archive photographique. Dans tous ces cas, le public doit pouvoir identifier immediatement la nature de l'image. Quand faut-il eviter les images generees par IA ? La prudence doit etre particulierement importante lorsqu'il s'agit d'illustrer des faits d'actualite. Pour une attaque, une manifestation, un accident, une catastrophe naturelle ou une crise humanitaire, il faut etre prudent avec l'utilisation des images generees. Il en va de meme pour les personnes reelles, notamment les victimes, les temoins, les responsables politiques ou les militaires. Leur representation artificielle dans une situation qu'elles n'ont pas vecue peut creer une confusion et porter atteinte a leur image. Dans ces situations, les medias doivent privilegier les images authentiques, les photos d'archives clairement datees et contextualisees, les cartes ou les infographies. Une image d'illustration peut egalement etre utilisee, mais elle doit etre choisie de maniere a ne pas etre confondue avec une photographie de l'evenement. La transparence, une exigence journalistique Lorsqu'une redaction decide d'utiliser une image generee par l'intelligence artificielle, elle doit clairement informer le public. Une legende telle que « Illustration generee par intelligence artificielle » permet de signaler la nature du visuel. Pour une reconstitution, la mention « Reconstitution generee par IA » peut egalement preciser qu'il ne s'agit pas d'une archive photographique. Cependant, la transparence ne justifie pas toutes les utilisations. Une image artificielle qui donne une representation trompeuse d'un evenement reel reste un mauvais choix editorial, meme lorsqu'elle porte une mention explicative. L'objectif n'est donc pas d'interdire systematiquement l'intelligence artificielle, mais de definir les limites de son utilisation dans la production journalistique. L’article Images IA, pourquoi leur utilisation peut tromper le public ? est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: CDF Munir, Sudan's interior minister discuss avenues to enhance bilateral cooperation: ISPR
items.description: Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Sudan’s Interior Minister Lieutenant General (Police) Babiker Samra Mustafa Ali on Friday discussed avenues to enhance bilateral cooperation between their countries. Lt Gen Ali called on CDF Munir at General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi during his visit to Pakistan, according to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR). “During the meeting, matters of mutual interest, evolving regional and global security dynamics and avenues for enhancing bilateral cooperation were discussed,” the statement said. “Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening relations between the two countries, particularly in the fields of security, counterterrorism and institutional cooperation.” The visiting dignitary “appreciated Pakistan’s role in promoting regional peace and stability and acknowledged the longstanding fraternal ties between Pakistan and Sudan”, according to ISPR. CDF Munir reaffirmed Pakistan’s desire to “further deepen bilateral engagement with Sudan and underscored the importance of close cooperation in addressing shared security challenges”. Earlier in the day, Ali called on Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. DPM Dar “reaffirmed Pakistan’s steadfast support for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity”, the Foreign Office said. He underscored the importance Pakistan attached to its relations with Sudan and its commitment to further strengthening the brotherly ties between the two countries. Meanwhile, the Sudanese minister expressed his “appreciation for Pakistan’s support and continued solidarity with Sudan”. “He highlighted the strength of brotherly relations between the two nations and underscored Sudan’s desire to further deepen cooperation across areas of mutual interest.” Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also attended the meeting. Meeting with PM Shehbaz On Thursday, a delegation led by Lt Gen Ali had met PM Shehbaz Sharif at the PM House. The premier affirmed that Pakistan attaches “great importance to its longstanding and fraternal relations” with Khartoum, the PM’s Office (PMO) said. “We want Sudan to emerge from its current crisis as a peaceful, stable, and prosperous country,” he was quoted as saying, expressing Pakistan’s desire to strengthen trade and investment ties with the North African country. “There are vast opportunities for bilateral cooperation in sectors such as agriculture, defence, education, and others,” the prime minister added. The Sudanese minister expressed gratitude to the premier for the humanitarian and medical assistance provided by the Pakistani government and people during difficult times, according to PMO. He also commended Pakistan’s support on international forums regarding efforts to restore peace and security in Sudan. Sudan remains the ​world’s largest displacement crisis more than three years after war broke out in 2023, when the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces clashed over issues including how to ​integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule. Around 8.6 million ​people remain displaced within the country, while more than 4.6m have fled across borders. ‌More ⁠than 5.2m people have also returned to their areas of origin, often finding homes, infrastructure and basic services destroyed.

items.title: RDC : lancement d’une réforme numérique pour renforcer la transparence judiciaire
items.description: La Republique democratique du Congo (RDC) a officiellement lance, le 5 novembre, un programme de modernisation de son systeme judiciaire, portant sur la numerisation des recettes de justice et l'interconnexion des juridictions, des parquets et des etablissements penitentiaires. La ceremonie, organisee au Palais de la Justice a Kinshasa, a ete presidee par le ministre d'etat, ministre de la Justice et garde des Sceaux, Guillaume Ngefa Atondoko Andali, en presence du ministre de l'economie numerique, Augustin Kibassa Maliba, de l'ambassadeur de l'Union europeenne en RDC, Douglas Darius Carpenter, et du representant resident du Programme des Nations unies pour le developpement (PNUD), Kamil Kayode Kamaluddeen. Portee par le gouvernement congolais avec l'appui technique du PNUD et le soutien financier de l'Union europeenne, cette reforme s'inscrit dans le Programme conjoint d'appui a la reforme de la justice en RDC pour la periode 2025-2029, precise un communique publie le 6 novembre par le PNUD. Numerisation : transparence et coordination judiciaires Le nouveau dispositif vise a remplacer progressivement les mecanismes manuels de perception des frais de justice par un systeme de paiement numerique securise, tracable et verifiable. Les autorites competentes pourront ainsi disposer de donnees fiables sur les recettes percues, les juridictions concernees et les transactions effectuees. Cette evolution devrait egalement reduire les risques de surfacturation, de perceptions irregulieres et de perte des justificatifs de paiement. Le second volet prevoit l'interconnexion des juridictions, des parquets et des etablissements penitentiaires grâce a une infrastructure numerique commune et securisee. L'objectif est de faciliter les echanges d'informations, d'ameliorer la coordination entre les institutions et d'assurer une meilleure continuite des services. Pour Guillaume Ngefa Atondoko Andali, « la digitalisation des recettes judiciaires et l'interconnexion de nos institutions constituent une avancee decisive dans la construction d'une justice moderne, transparente et credible ». Le ministre a souligne que cette reforme devait renforcer la redevabilite des institutions, securiser les ressources publiques et rapprocher la justice des citoyens. Il a egalement appele a un suivi rigoureux pour garantir une amelioration concrete des services rendus aux justiciables. Le PNUD et l'Union europeenne ont reaffirme leur soutien a la modernisation de la justice congolaise. « La technologie doit etre un levier d'efficacite, d'inclusion et de confiance », a declare le representant resident du PNUD, Kamil Kayode Kamaluddeen. Il a souligne la necessite de securiser les recettes publiques, de renforcer les capacites nationales et de former les utilisateurs afin de garantir la perennite du dispositif.

items.title: L’immigration au Japon, entre impératif économique et résistance sociétale
items.description: À télécharger Lire la note (PDF) Avec plus de quatre millions de résidents étrangers et une population qui a perdu plus de trois millions d’habitants en cinq ans, le Japon n’a jamais autant dépendu de la main-d’œuvre venue de l’extérieur. C’est pourtant le moment qu’a choisi le gouvernement de Takaichi Sanae pour durcir l’accès à la naturalisation, au séjour permanent et à la propriété foncière. Perçu à l’étranger comme un raidissement nationaliste, ce tournant relève moins d’une fermeture que d’une dissociation. La porte s’ouvre plus largement au travail, elle se referme sur l’installation. Cette note en retrace la genèse, en analyse la réception dans une société plus ambivalente qu’il n’y paraît et en évalue les effets possibles sur la cohésion du pays comme sur son attractivité internationale. L’article L’immigration au Japon, entre impératif économique et résistance sociétale est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Sansy Kaba Diakité révolutionne la littérature jeunesse avec son livre audio « N’fa, le fils de Kankoula »
items.description: ​À l'occasion du Salon international du livre jeunesse, l'auteur et éditeur Sansy Kaba Diakité a marqué les esprits en présentant sa toute dernière création : un livre audio adapté de sa bande dessinée intitulée « N'fa, le fils de Kankoula ». ​Pensé comme une véritable innovation, ce format audio a pour objectif principal d'attirer les enfants et les jeunes guinéens vers la lecture. En écoutant cette œuvre thématisée et rythmée par des créations artistiques fantastiques, le public est incité à découvrir les textes originaux en librairie, selon Sansy Kaba Diakité. ​« En écoutant ce livre, cette bande dessinée, ils auront envie de découvrir le texte lui-même, d'aller chercher dans les librairies le livre. Donc c'est ça l'objectif : faire en sorte que les Guinéens se mettent à la lecture », explique l'auteur. ​Séduit par la qualité de cette réalisation immersive, le Directeur général de L'Harmattan Guinée souligne que ce support résonne particulièrement auprès du public local. Les auditeurs s'approprient d'autant plus l'histoire qu'elle prend racine dans l'histoire de la Guinée, de Kankan, de Kèfina et de Kabada. ​Inspirée des récits transmis par ses grands-parents, l'œuvre lève le voile sur les origines des communautés et des familles de la région. L'auteur y explore notamment l'histoire des Kaba, venus de Diafounou entre la Mauritanie et le Mali, et leurs alliances historiques avec les Condé de Kankan. ​À travers ce projet, l'écrivain et éditeur combat l'adage africain selon lequel « un vieillard qui meurt est une bibliothèque qui brûle ». En couchant ces récits oraux d'abord en prose, puis en bande dessinée, et enfin en livre audio, il offre aux plus jeunes un accès ludique à leur arbre généalogique et à leur patrimoine culturel. ​Aux dires de Sansy Kaba Diakité, c​e premier tome audio marque le début d'une grande aventure éditoriale. Deux autres tomes sont d'ores et déjà en préparation pour compléter cette trilogie, avec des projets axés sur l'avenir de la Guinée. Une initiative saluée qui redéfinit les codes de la transmission intergénérationnelle à l'ère du numérique et de l'audio.

items.title: El Menfi de Meriem Guemache : le drame des déportés algériens en Nouvelle-Calédonie
items.description: Après l’Absente , recueil de nouvelles paru en 2023, l’écrivaine et journaliste Meriem Guemache signe son retour avec un nouveau roman présenté lors du Salon international du livre d’Alger ( SILA 2026 , 29 octobre – 7 novembre). Intitulé El Menfi (Le banni), ce livre paru chez Casbah Editions revisite le drame des déportés algériens en Nouvelle-Calédonie, au 19 -ème siècle. Meriem Guemache exhume cette histoire oubliée et raconte des destins fracassés par la colonisation française. Après les insurrections de 1871, des milliers d’Algériens à l’instar de Boumezrag, El Mokrani et de Aziz Ben Cheikh El Haddad ont été déportés en Nouvelle-Calédonie, sur ce ‘caillou’ du Pacifique, île des antipodes. Slimane, personnage principal du roman de Meriem Guemache, n'a que 24 ans lorsqu’il est jugé par la Cour d’assise coloniale de Constantine et condamné aux travaux forcés, sur l’île Nou. Son tort : s’être révolté contre l’expropriation de ses terres à Bordj Bou Arreridj au profit des colons. Algériens déportés en Nouvelle-Calédonie : des condamnés réduits à un simple numéro d’écrou « A travers l’histoire de Slimane, je redonne une voix à tous ces Algériens qui ont été arrachés à leur famille, à leur pays, pour être acheminés sur des bateaux, à l’autre bout du monde et y être exploité jusqu’à épuisement, dans l’enfer du bagne de l’île Nou (Nouméa- Nouvelle Calédonie). Slimane est un père, un mari, un fils, un frère mais du jour au lendemain, il est réduit à simple numéro d’écrou. L’enfant de Bordj Bou Arreridj, subira la politique d’humiliation et d’avilissement imposée par le pouvoir colonial français », explique Meriem Guemache. Sur le Calvados, en route vers la Nouvelle-Calédonie, depuis Brest (Bretagne) les transportés vivent dans des cales insalubres pendant près de cinq mois. « Victimes de scorbut, d’anémie, de malnutrition, beaucoup n’arriveront jamais à Nouméa. Leurs cadavres sont jetés par-dessus bord. Dans la première partie de mon roman, je décris cette traversée cauchemardesque marquée par la faim, les maladies, le manque d’hygiène, la promiscuité et les caprices d’une météo musclée sans oublier la cruauté et le mépris des surveillants à bord du trois-mâts », dévoile l’écrivaine. Quand Slimane et ses camarades d’infortunes débarquent en Nouvelle-Calédonie, ils ressemblent à des spectres. Des êtres décharnés et complétement désorientés. Extrait : « (…) ces silhouettes qui sortent du bateau comme du ventre de l’enfer, sales, déguenillées, ensauvagées. Ce ne sont pas des hommes. Juste des êtres déshumanisé et dépossédés de leur dignité par le système colonial ». Les lecteurs pourront partager l’existence de Slimane dans cette colonie de peuplement pénale. « On va se plonger dans le quotidien de tous les forçats algériens transportés en Nouvelle-Calédonie tout en faisant la différence entre les déportés simples (les chefs politiques) et les transportés (condamnés de droit communs). Comment vivaient-ils ? Comment étaient-ils traités par l’administration coloniale française, quelles relations entretenaient-ils avec les Communards de Paris, eux aussi déportés après les révoltes de 1871 ? Vont-ils se marier, avoir des enfants ? Si oui, comment pourront ils transmettre leur héritage culturel et rester fidèles à leurs origines et à leur identité ? ». Un long travail de recherche « El Menfi est le fruit de deux années d’écriture et de travail, précise Meriem Guemache. C’est une fiction basée sur des faits historiques vérifiés et recoupés. « Avant de me lancer dans l’écriture de ce livre, j’ai consacré plusieurs mois à me documenter. J’ai essayé de lire tout ce qui a été publié sur ce sujet. Les ouvrages d’écrivains et chercheurs algériens comme Mehdi Lallaoui, Melica Ouennougui, ou Rachid Sellal m’ont beaucoup éclairée. J’ai aussi regardé des vidéos et des documentaires sur Internet, je me suis aussi intéressée aux témoignages des descendants qui vivent toujours là- bas ainsi qu’à ceux des Communards, qui ont été déportés en Nouvelle-Calédonie après leur soulèvement en 1871 : Louise Michel, Henri Rochefort, Olivier Pain, Jean Allemane… Après les amnisties de 1889 et 1890 et leur retour en France, ils se sont mobilisés pour alerter l’opinion publique sur le sort des Algériens retenus en Nouvelle- Calédonie ». Pour donner à son roman une dimension romanesque, l’auteure a dû étudier d’autres détails. « Je me suis documentée sur la météo de ces îles tropicales, sur la faune, la flore, et j’ai retracé étape par étape, la traversée des bateaux bagnes depuis le port de Brest : Tenerife (Océan Atlantique), Dakar, île Sainte Catherine (Brésil) et enfin Nouméa ». L’histoire des Algériens déportés en Nouvelle-Calédonie « devrait être enseignée dans les écoles » L’histoire des déportés et transportés en Nouvelle -Calédonie a toujours interpellé cette écrivaine et journaliste. « Cette histoire est vraiment bouleversante. J’ai souvent croisé des gens qui m’ont parlé d’un parent condamné à la déportation sur cet île lointaine. Il est de notre devoir de préserver la mémoire et de ne jamais oublier ces hommes arrachés, à leur patrie, à la fleur de l’âge. Ils avaient tous des familles qu’il chérissait et pour lesquels ils comptaient aussi. Des parents, une fratrie, une épouse, des enfants, des cousins… Et puis, du jour au lendemain, ces hommes se sont retrouvés à l’autre bout du monde, déracinés, humiliés, affamés…Cette histoire devrait être enseignée dans les écoles car elle n’est pas connue. C’est un devoir de mémoire », explique-t-elle. Dis à ma mère de ne pas pleurer Dans El Menfi Meriem Guemache fait un clin d’œil à la célèbre chanson popularisée par Akli Yahiètene ‘El Menfi’. Aux abords du cimetière de Nessadiou à Bourail où reposent les corps des bannis, monte un lamento qui nous déchire les entrailles. « Assis devant l’entrée du mausolée de Sidi Moulay, Tayeb entonne son chant mélancolique : Goulou’lemmi’ma’tebkich, ya el menfi, ouldek’ rebbi’ maykhhelich’che, ya el menfi « Dites à ma mère de ne pas pleurer, ô banni, Dieu n’abandonnera pas ton fils, ô banni ». El Menfi de Meriem Guemache, un roman profondément bouleversant qui ravive la mémoire de tous ces bannis de l’Histoire et exhume, des profondeurs de l’oubli, une page tragique de notre histoire coloniale ». El Menfi. Meriem Guemache. Casbah Editions. Octobre 2026. 141 p. 1000 DA L’article El Menfi de Meriem Guemache : le drame des déportés algériens en Nouvelle-Calédonie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Le Porc au piqué : L’innovation culinaire d’Augustin Nikiéma
items.description: De nombreux visiteurs de la 18ᵉ édition du SIAO sont attirés par l’espace gastronomique surtout par le Porc au piqué, une spécialité culinaire d’Augustin Nikiéma. Le SIAO, ce sont aussi des mets délicieux proposés aux visiteurs à l'espace gastronomique. Cette année, plusieurs recettes attirent l’attention notamment le Porc au piqué de Augustin Nikiéma, un ingénieur géomètre-topographe. Il n’a pas hésité à stopper temporairement ses chantiers pour s'installer au SIAO pour faire connaitre sa technique de cuisiner le porc. La préparation du Porc au piqué consiste, a-t-il expliqué, à embrocher l'animal sur une broche rotative automatisée. Selon Augustin Nikiéma, le SIAO est un carrefour d'opportunités propice aux rencontres d'affaires et au partage d'expériences Cuit lentement pendant au moins deux heures sur un charbon ardent, le porc subit une transformation. « La graisse fond entièrement et la peau devient aussi croustillante qu'un biscuit. Il s'agit d'une véritable alternative saine et savoureuse qui élimine l’excès de gras souvent reproché aux autres modes de cuisson », a-t-il affirmé. Julien Zoungrana Crédit photo : Julien ZOUNGRANA

items.title: 4ème session ordinaire de la commune Lacs 1 : Un budget primitif de plus de 628 millions FCFA approuvé
items.description: Aného, 6 nov. (ATOP)-Les conseillers municipaux de la commune Lacs 1 ont adopté, le vendredi 5 novembre, un budget primitif équilibré en recettes et en dépenses à 628 954 110 FCFA pour l’exercice 2027. Le budget a été approuvé au terme de la quatrième session ordinaire de l’année, ouverte le 27 octobre dernier. Il se répartit en deux grandes sections. Le fonctionnement est évalué à 479 224 877 FCFA, tandis que les investissements s’élèvent à 149 729 233 FCFA. A travers ces prévisions budgétaires, la municipalité entend poursuivre progressivement la réalisation des infrastructures prioritaires, renforcer l’accès des populations aux services sociaux de base et améliorer les capacités de fonctionnement de son administration. Dans le domaine des infrastructures routières, le conseil municipal a retenu le reprofilage des voies d’accès ouvertes en 2025 pour les rendre plus fonctionnelles. Déjà électrifiées, ces voies demeurent difficilement praticables en raison de l’absence de chargement. En matière de santé, la commune prévoit la construction d’un hangar au sein d’une Unité de soins périphériques (USP). Cette infrastructure permettra d’offrir un meilleur cadre d’accueil aux femmes lors des séances de vaccination et des activités de sensibilisation. Pour le secteur de l’éducation, la commune compte construire un bâtiment scolaire comprenant trois salles de classe, un bureau et un magasin, ainsi que la dotation en mobilier au profit d’un établissement confronté à un besoin pressant d’infrastructures. Par ailleurs, l’extension des réseaux d’eau et d’électricité figure parmi les préoccupations des élus locaux. La municipalité entend aussi poursuivre ses efforts en matière d’éclairage public, à travers l’installation de lampadaires solaires dans les villages qui ne disposent pas encore de cet équipement. Le maire, Me Alexis Coffi Aquereburu a assisté aux travaux. ATOP/AAK/MG/BV

items.title: Modernisation de l’administration : le ministre Bourouno multiplie les partenariats et porte les réformes guinéennes à l’international
items.description: Le ministre de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique, Faya François Bourouno, a effectué une série de rencontres et de démarches diplomatiques en marge de plusieurs rendez-vous internationaux, notamment à Abidjan, en Côte d’Ivoire, et à Bakou, en Azerbaïdjan. Au cœur de cette mission : le renforcement des compétences des agents publics, le partage d’expériences avec d’autres pays et la promotion des réformes engagées par la Guinée pour moderniser son administration. Le 2 novembre 2026, à Abidjan, en marge du Forum des leaders organisé par HEC Montréal, le ministre Bourouno, à la tête d’une délégation de son département, a échangé avec les responsables de cette institution sur les perspectives de coopération dans le domaine de la formation. À cette occasion, la délégation guinéenne a présenté les avancées enregistrées dans le cadre de la réforme de la Fonction publique, notamment à travers le Fichier unique de gestion administrative et de la solde (FUGAS) et le Référentiel des métiers et des compétences. Ces outils visent à améliorer la gestion des ressources humaines de l’État et à mieux adapter les profils des agents aux besoins de l’administration. Intéressée par ces initiatives, HEC Montréal a manifesté son intérêt pour un partenariat avec la Direction générale de la Fonction publique et l’École nationale d’administration de Guinée. Cette collaboration envisagée devrait notamment permettre d’identifier les besoins de formation, de renforcer les capacités des agents publics et de développer la formation de formateurs guinéens. Trois jours plus tard, le 5 novembre, à Bakou, en Azerbaïdjan, Faya François Bourouno a pris part, à la tête d’une délégation guinéenne, au panel ministériel intitulé « L’avenir de la gouvernance : vision, mission et transformation », organisé dans le cadre du Sommet des Nations unies sur l’innovation dans la gouvernance. Devant les participants à cette rencontre internationale, le ministre a présenté la vision guinéenne de la transformation de l’État, en mettant particulièrement l’accent sur le programme Simandou 2040. Structuré autour de 122 mégaprojets et de 36 réformes stratégiques, ce programme constitue, selon la présentation faite par le ministre, le socle de la transformation structurelle du pays. Il ambitionne notamment de faire de la croissance économique un levier durable d’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations, grâce à des services publics plus accessibles et mieux adaptés aux attentes des citoyens. Le ministre a également exposé plusieurs réformes engagées pour améliorer le fonctionnement de l’administration publique, valoriser le capital humain de l’État et renforcer la qualité des prestations offertes aux usagers. Parmi les initiatives présentées figurent le Guichet unique des services publics (GUSP), le Répertoire national des emplois et des compétences ainsi que le Baromètre national des services publics. En marge de ce sommet, le ministre Faya François Bourouno, a également eu un entretien avec son homologue gabonaise, Laurence Ndong, ministre de la Fonction publique et du Renforcement des capacités de la République gabonaise. Les échanges ont porté sur les expériences respectives des deux pays en matière de réforme et de modernisation de l’administration publique. À cette occasion, Faya François Bourouno a présenté les principales avancées de la Guinée, notamment la fiabilisation des effectifs de l’État, l’intégration de la gestion administrative et de la solde, la dématérialisation progressive des procédures ainsi que les travaux de définition des emplois et des compétences. Il a également mis en avant le Guichet unique des services publics, destiné à renforcer l’interconnexion des administrations et à simplifier les démarches des usagers. De son côté, la ministre gabonaise a partagé les expériences de son pays en matière de régularisation des carrières, d’évaluation des performances des agents publics, de recrutement par concours et de développement du portail e-Fonction publique. La réforme du parcours de retraite a également été évoquée comme une illustration des efforts visant à alléger les démarches administratives des citoyens, en confiant à l’administration la coordination de procédures auparavant supportées par les usagers. À l’issue de cette rencontre, les deux ministres ont exprimé leur volonté de poursuivre les échanges techniques et de renforcer leur coopération. Dans cette perspective, une visite de travail en Guinée a été proposée et favorablement accueillie par la partie gabonaise, afin d’approfondir le partage d’expériences et d’explorer de nouvelles pistes de collaboration. À travers ces différentes rencontres à Abidjan et à Bakou, la mission du ministre Faya François Bourouno a ainsi permis de mettre en avant les réformes administratives engagées en Guinée, tout en ouvrant des perspectives de coopération avec des institutions de formation et des administrations partenaires. L'objectif affiché est de contribuer à la construction d'une fonction publique davantage fondée sur les compétences, l’innovation, la performance et l’amélioration continue du service rendu aux citoyens. Youssouf Keita L’article Modernisation de l’administration : le ministre Bourouno multiplie les partenariats et porte les réformes guinéennes à l’international est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Burkina : Plus de 7 000 rapatriés de Guinée attendus
items.description: Le Conseil régional de secours d’urgence et de réhabilitation (CORESUR) du Kadiogo a tenu une réunion d'urgence ce vendredi 6 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou pour coordonner l'accueil des Burkinabè expulsés de Guinée. Au total, plus de 7 000 personnes sont concernées. L’afflux des Burkinabè expulsés de la Guinée nécessite une mobilisation urgente des structures de secours et des autorités régionales. Au 5 novembre 2026, 3 533 personnes étaient déjà enregistrées à Koloko et Bobo-Dioulasso : 2 428 hommes, 209 femmes et 896 enfants. Ce vendredi, les premiers cars sont arrivés à Bobo-Dioulasso et une cinquantaine d'autres étaient annoncés, avec environ 4 000 personnes supplémentaires attendues au petit matin. Le Gouvernement a dépêché plus de 150 cars en République du Mali, auxquels s'ajoutent une dizaine de camions pour les effets personnels. Présidée par le Gouverneur Abdoulaye Bassinga, la réunion a acté que les rapatriés originaires de Banfora, Dédougou ou de localités proches rejoindront directement leurs destinations depuis Bobo-Dioulasso. Ouagadougou sera un deuxième site de transit pour les régions du Kadiogo, des Koulsé, du Liptako, du Soum, du Nakambé, du Nazinon, du Goulmou, du Sirba et du Tapoa. Pour ce qui concerne, l'organisation, plusieurs commissions sont mises en place : accueil et hébergement, santé (avec l'appui de la Croix-Rouge), sécurité (Police et Gendarmerie), hygiène et assainissement, assistance alimentaire, logistique, réception et distribution des dons, ainsi qu'une commission de coordination. Nadège KINDA Minute.bf

Régions : Le Guiriko expose le Kôkô Donda, et Liptako des bijoux de prestige
items.description: Au cœur de la 18e édition du SIAO, les stands des régions du Guiriko et du Liptako mettent en lumière la richesse et la diversité des produits du terroir burkinabè. La région du Guiriko mise sur la valorisation de son potentiel agricole, agroalimentaire et textile. Les étagères regorgent de produits forestiers non ligneux transformés, notamment des mangues séchées, des infusions de kinkeliba, du miel et des huiles locales conditionnées. Côté vestimentaire, l'accent est mis sur le patrimoine textile avec des tenues confectionnées en pagne traditionnel et en Kôkô Dunda aux motifs colorés. La bijouterie de la région du Liptako séduit de nombreux visiteurs Au Liptako, la région se distingue dans le domaine de l'artisanat d'art et de la bijouterie. Les vitrines exposent une grande variété de bijoux de prestige finement travaillés. Les visiteurs y découvrent des colliers, des bagues, des boucles d'oreilles et des bracelets massifs étincelants, conçus essentiellement en argent et des parures ornées de perles traditionnelles. Cette proximité géographique dans les pavillons du salon donne lieu à des échanges animés entre les exposants des deux localités. Derrière cette saine émulation commerciale se cache en réalité une longue tradition de parenté à plaisanterie qui permet aux représentants du Guiriko et du Liptako de se lancer des joutes verbales humoristiques. items.title: Zio / Changement climatique : Les membres des comités régional et de coordination du plan d’adaptation installés
items.description: Tsévié, 6 nov. (ATOP) – Les membres des comités régional et de coordination du Plan régional d’adaptation (PRA) au changement climatique de la région Maritime ont été installés, le jeudi 5 novembre à Tsévié. La cérémonie a été présidée par le gouverneur Taïrou Bagbiègue. Composé de 19 membres, le comité régional est chargé de donner des orientations stratégiques, de suivre les progrès de la mise en œuvre du plan et de définir les modalités techniques et financières nécessaires à sa durabilité. Il est placé sous la responsabilité du gouverneur. Le comité de coordination, qui compte 13 membres assure la mise en œuvre des actions, prépare les documents du plan et les soumet à l’approbation. Il est dirigé par le secrétaire général du gouvernorat, Dotsè Médjina. Les deux structures ont un mandat de cinq ans, couvrant la période 2026-2030. Le PRA repose sur trois axes : l’adaptation climatique, l’agriculture, la foresterie et les ressources en eau, ainsi que la résilience des territoires et des communautés. Son coût global prévisionnel est estimé à 16,930 milliards de FCFA. La cérémonie d’installation a été précédée de deux communications consacrées aux orientations du plan et aux acteurs chargés de sa mise en œuvre. A cette occasion, le gouverneur Bagbiègue a rappelé que la région Maritime, comme les autres régions du Togo, subit les effets des aléas climatiques. Il a salué l’appui de l’Organisation des Nations unies pour l’alimentation et l’agriculture (FAO) aux initiatives d’adaptation. Il a invité les membres des comités à travailler dans l’intérêt des populations. Les membres des comités préfectoraux et communaux des plans d’adaptation au changement climatique de la région Maritime seront installés dans les prochains jours. ATOP/BBG/AO/BV
